Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar and her husband Dr Gregory Bissessar years ago.

KEVON FELMINE
Se­nior Re­porter
kevon.felmine@guardian.co.tt

A car crash weeks be­fore the 2025 gen­er­al elec­tion left Dr Gre­go­ry Bisses­sar with in­juries that still af­fect his walk­ing, his wife, Prime Min­is­ter Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar, re­vealed yes­ter­day.
Per­sad-Bisses­sar ad­dressed the long-run­ning ques­tion of his ab­sence from her side at the Siparia Women’s As­so­ci­a­tion an­nu­al Di­vali cel­e­bra­tion at the Siparia Con­stituen­cy Of­fice in Pe­nal last night.
“Many peo­ple keep ask­ing where he is. Gre­go­ry can­not join us tonight.”
The crash hap­pened a few weeks be­fore the elec­tion as they were head­ing to San­gre Grande, when an­oth­er ve­hi­cle col­lid­ed with the cou­ple’s car. The Prime Min­is­ter said the in­juries have not dimmed her hus­band.
“His great spir­it and im­mense brain­pow­er re­main strong.”
The dis­clo­sure came af­ter a re­li­gious cer­e­mo­ny and a pro­ces­sion from Clarke Road to the of­fice. Cab­i­net min­is­ters, a may­or, re­gion­al cor­po­ra­tion and state board chair­men, coun­cil­lors, na­tion­al awardees, per­ma­nent sec­re­taries and devo­tees walked with her in a fes­tive re­li­gious show­case.
At the podi­um, she de­liv­ered a very pub­lic mes­sage to her hus­band.
“Gre­go­ry, thank you for your courage, your pa­tience and your un­wa­ver­ing love. I could not have made this jour­ney with­out you.”
She called him her rock and a steady light through the de­mands and dif­fi­cul­ties of pub­lic life.
Per­sad-Bisses­sar said she was shar­ing the fam­i­ly mat­ter be­cause many in the au­di­ence were car­ing for some­one they love. She turned to the Holy Ra­mayana, re­call­ing how Si­ta and Lak­sh­man ac­com­pa­nied Ra­ma in­to for­est ex­ile while his broth­er Bharat held the king­dom in trust for his re­turn. Their love, she said, was ex­pressed in the re­spon­si­bil­i­ties they car­ried for one an­oth­er.
“Cher­ish those who stand be­side you through hard­ship.”
The love that sus­tains fam­i­lies, she added, al­so strength­ens the com­mu­ni­ties they be­long to.
Re­flect­ing on her per­son­al jour­ney, she point­ed across the road to the Pe­nal Mar­ket, where, as a lit­tle girl, she stood be­side her grand­moth­er, whom she called Aagie, sell­ing bo­di and oth­er veg­eta­bles to help the fam­i­ly make a liv­ing. She said she nev­er imag­ined she would one day stand across from it as Prime Min­is­ter, cel­e­brat­ing Di­vali with the chil­dren and grand­chil­dren of the peo­ple who helped raise her.
She said her Gov­ern­ment must re­pay that debt in ser­vice. Re­li­able wa­ter, ac­ces­si­ble health­care, prop­er­ly main­tained roads, ed­u­ca­tion and op­por­tu­ni­ties to earn, she said, are the foun­da­tions of se­cure fam­i­ly life, and the Bud­get and the work of Min­istries must serve that pur­pose, es­pe­cial­ly in com­mu­ni­ties that have wait­ed longest. She al­so pledged ac­tion against crime, cor­rup­tion and ne­glect.
It has been 31 years since she first be­came the area’s Mem­ber of Par­lia­ment and 29 years since the Di­vali tra­di­tion be­gan.
“You will have my ser­vice, my strength and my heart to the end of my days.”
The As­so­ci­a­tion, which has host­ed the func­tion for 29 years, ho­n­oured sev­er­al res­i­dents. Awardees in­clud­ed crick­eter Am­ri­ta Ram­ta­hal, foot­baller Dar­rel Gar­cia, seam­stress and teacher Carmi­na Ho­sein, pub­lic ser­vant Vi­jai Bridglal and agri­cul­tur­al­ist De­nesh Tar­soo. Stu­dents Au­rea Ma­habir, Dev­ina Do­dal, Kadir Chung and Kavir New­ton were al­so recog­nised.

title: Questions over who organised, funded Parliament Divali event
summary: Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar presents Opposition Leader Pennelope Beckles with a gift, alongside House Speaker Jagdeo Singh and Senate President Wade Mark at the Divali celebrations held at P

An event to mark Di­vali cel­e­bra­tions at Par­lia­ment, which the Prime Min­is­ter and her min­is­ters claim as his­toric, has raised ques­tions about who or­gan­ised and fund­ed it.
Both House Speak­er Jagdeo Singh and Deputy Speak­er Dr Aiy­na Ali told Guardian Me­dia that the Par­lia­ment staff or­gan­ised the event.
How­ev­er, Colleen Hold­er, Par­lia­ment’s Di­rec­tor of Cor­po­rate Com­mu­ni­ca­tions and Pro­duc­tions, told the me­dia yes­ter­day that it was an out­side event which they fa­cil­i­tat­ed.
“While the event was held at the Par­lia­ment, it was not or­gan­ised by the Par­lia­ment,” she told the me­dia yes­ter­day.
When con­tact­ed, Singh said: “I had noth­ing to do with the fund­ing or the arrange­ments of it. That is the Par­lia­ment staff.”
For her part, when con­tact­ed, Ali ini­tial­ly told Guardian Me­dia that Par­lia­ment or­gan­ised it.
How­ev­er, when pressed fur­ther about her role, Ali said she helped with the plan­ning and co-or­di­na­tion of the event. When asked about fund­ing for the event, she said she did not have those an­swers but that in­for­ma­tion could be ob­tained through the Free­dom of In­for­ma­tion Act (FOIA).
Hold­er de­scribed it as a “spillover from the sit­ting.”
Asked specif­i­cal­ly by Guardian Me­dia who fund­ed it, Hold­er re­spond­ed: “It was not or­gan­ised by Par­lia­ment, so I can­not say.”
The event, which in­clud­ed both the Gov­ern­ment and Op­po­si­tion mem­bers as well as chil­dren, was held on Fri­day fol­low­ing the con­clu­sion of the day’s sit­ting of the House of Rep­re­sen­ta­tives. It was joint­ly host­ed by Singh and Sen­ate Pres­i­dent Wade Mark.
Ac­cord­ing to so­cial me­dia posts by Par­lia­ment, state tele­vi­sion sta­tion TTT, MPs Bar­ry Padarath and Sad­dam Ho­sein, the event in­clud­ed speech­es by Prime Min­is­ter Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar and Op­po­si­tion Leader Pen­ne­lope Beck­les, a re-en­act­ment of Ram­leela, deya light­ing and a pa­rade of mur­tis (stat­ues of Hin­du Gods) on trucks along Aber­crom­bie Street. At the event, Beck­les-Robin­son was gift­ed a to­ken from the Prime Min­is­ter.
A hand in stag­ing
In seek­ing to dis­tin­guish Par­lia­ment’s role in the host­ing of the event, Hold­er ex­plained that oth­er sim­i­lar events are usu­al­ly held at Par­lia­ment.
“The event was held at the Red House. Con­sul­ta­tion took place be­tween Par­lia­ment staff and the pre­sid­ing of­fi­cers as al­ways hap­pens with such events,” she said. She ob­served that Par­lia­ment host­ed a creche bless­ing event in the same court­yard last year, al­so in con­sul­ta­tion with the pre­sid­ing of­fi­cers.
Asked by Guardian Me­dia to iden­ti­fy the or­gan­is­er of the Di­vali event, Hold­er re­spond­ed: “I do not have that in­for­ma­tion” but that they “are in the know and had a hand in stag­ing.”
In the past, she not­ed, Par­lia­ment host­ed many events by or­gan­i­sa­tions which are not di­rect­ly re­lat­ed to the Par­lia­ment, like the First Peo­ples’ smoke cer­e­mo­ny, which hap­pens on Oc­to­ber 12 every year.
“Once the req­ui­site re­quests are made, dis­cus­sions held and ap­provals grant­ed. It is af­ter all the Peo­ple’s Par­lia­ment,” she said. Most re­cent­ly, Par­lia­ment host­ed the an­niver­sary launch/dis­cus­sion of the TTPS 1990 doc­u­men­tary and every Thurs­day, it hosts wed­dings on be­half of the Min­istry of Le­gal Af­fairs.
Asked then, if Par­lia­ment didn’t or­gan­ise it, whether a host­ing fee was paid, she re­spond­ed: “The Par­lia­ment is not a re­ceiv­er of rev­enue, so no fees are paid. As I in­di­cat­ed, var­i­ous re­quests are made, dis­cus­sions held and re­quests may or may not be grant­ed. Each re­quest is con­sid­ered on its own.”
Par­lia­ment was al­lo­cat­ed $162 mil­lion in the 2027 Bud­get 2027.
At the event, Per­sad-Bisses­sar de­scribed it as a proud and mov­ing mo­ment as it marked 60 years since Di­vali was de­clared a pub­lic hol­i­day.
“To our chil­dren here and every­where, I say this: Par­lia­ment be­longs to you. You don’t need rich par­ents, or elite con­nects to mat­ter here. You mat­ter here to­day sim­ply be­cause you are a child of our beloved na­tion. Your name, your faith, your fam­i­ly’s in­come or where you live can nev­er make you less de­serv­ing of its care,” she said.
Mean­while, Beck­les ap­pealed for greater na­tion­al uni­ty.
“Our di­ver­si­ty is not our weak­ness; it is our great­est strength. As Leader of the Op­po­si­tion, I wish to make a spe­cial ap­peal to our na­tion on this sa­cred oc­ca­sion: let us choose uni­ty over di­vi­sion, let us choose un­der­stand­ing over tol­er­ance, and let us choose hope over de­spair,” Beck­les said.

SHAL­IZA HAS­SANALI
Se­nior In­ves­tiga­tive Re­porter
shal­iza.has­sanali@guardian.co.tt
A qui­et shift in the il­lic­it cig­a­rette trade from Suri­name to Trinidad could be one of the fac­tors fu­elling a boom­ing de­mand in pris­ons, where a sin­gle cig­a­rette can cost an in­mate up to $100.
These cig­a­rettes en­ter the pris­ons via drone drops.
In a sin­gle night, prison of­fi­cials said they have record­ed up to 50 drones fly­ing over the pris­ons to de­liv­er con­tra­band to pris­on­ers.
“It’s like they are work­ing a taxi ser­vice,” Prison Of­fi­cers As­so­ci­a­tion pres­i­dent Ger­ard Gor­don told Guardian Me­dia on Thurs­day, re­fer­ring to the drones’ fre­quent ac­tiv­i­ty.
“The is­sue of ad­dress­ing con­tra­band is a con­stant,” Gor­don said.
“It’s a lu­cra­tive busi­ness in prison.”
When of­fi­cers in­ter­rupt that trade, they come un­der at­tack.
On Au­gust 18, prison of­fi­cers said they in­ter­cept­ed an aer­i­al de­liv­ery of 16 car­tons of il­lic­it cig­a­rettes at the Max­i­mum Se­cu­ri­ty Prison in Arou­ca.
A stan­dard cig­a­rette car­ton con­tains ten packs to­talling 200 cig­a­rettes.
Prison of­fi­cials said these 16 car­tons could have raked in $320,000.
For this year, sev­er­al in­ter­cep­tions have been made.
If de­mand out­weighs sup­ply, Gor­don said, the cost of one cig­a­rette would in­crease.
He said an in­mate could pay as much as “$100” for a smug­gled cig­a­rette.
Cig­a­rettes are the world’s most il­lic­it­ly trad­ed prod­uct and can po­ten­tial­ly pro­vide the high­est rev­enue.
Two pop­u­lar ways of achiev­ing this are by pro­duc­ing and sell­ing coun­ter­feit cig­a­rettes and sourc­ing cig­a­rettes le­git­i­mate­ly pro­duced in one coun­try, then smug­gling them in­to a sec­ond coun­try for re­sale.
Dur­ing sev­er­al in­tel­li­gence-based se­cu­ri­ty op­er­a­tions this year, dozens of pack­ets of il­lic­it cig­a­rettes were al­so con­fis­cat­ed with­in the prison walls.
Mem­bers of the pub­lic al­so throw pro­hib­it­ed items over the walls at the Port-of-Spain Prison for in­mates.
“What we have been ad­vo­cat­ing for, of course, is the im­ple­men­ta­tion and use of tech­no­log­i­cal coun­ter­mea­sures with the use of drones,” Gor­don said.
Gor­don said the quan­ti­ty and weight of con­tra­band some drones car­ry amazes him.
He said prison of­fi­cers no longer take the chance to smug­gle con­tra­band in­to the pris­ons be­cause they are searched by the Prison In­ter­dic­tion Team and scanned up­on en­try.
“Those who get caught, I say good rid­dance.”
T&T now at cen­tre of il­lic­it trade
The shift of the il­lic­it cig­a­rette trade from Suri­name to Trinidad is con­tained in a 48-page re­port by C-Anal­i­sis, a Colom­bian-based com­pa­ny that pro­vides con­sul­tan­cy in se­cu­ri­ty is­sues, risk analy­sis, pub­lic pol­i­cy and rur­al de­vel­op­ment, which Guardian Me­dia ob­tained.
Da­ta pro­vid­ed in the re­port showed that in 2023, cig­a­rette trade in Suri­name was rough­ly US$25.3 mil­lion, while in Trinidad, the fig­ure stood at US$3.6 mil­lion.
By 2024, the re­port stat­ed that Suri­name’s trade had dropped to US$10 mil­lion, while “im­ports to Trinidad” rose to US$4.1 mil­lion.
“This da­ta should be con­sid­ered a min­i­mum, since smug­glers make big ef­forts to hide. Our main hy­poth­e­sis is that near­ly US$15 mil­lion that did not go to Suri­name in 2024 went to Trinidad in­stead and a large por­tion was un­der­re­port­ed,” the re­port said.
He said cig­a­rettes man­u­fac­tured in Paraguay, Viet­nam, Chi­na, In­dia, Ko­rea and South­east Asia are smug­gled in­to T&T, Grena­da, Guyana, and Suri­name.
The re­port, ti­tled “Memo 329-Trinidad and To­ba­go”, was re­leased in Sep­tem­ber 2026 by C-Anal­i­sis di­rec­tor Daniel Ri­co, who vis­it­ed Trinidad twice to in­ves­ti­gate the coun­try’s il­lic­it cig­a­rette trade.
What caught Ri­co’s at­ten­tion dur­ing his vis­it was a Trinida­di­an busi­ness­man’s link to 14 ship­ments of il­lic­it cig­a­rettes to­talling 32 con­tain­ers be­tween 2022 and 2023.
In Jan­u­ary 2025, at least 12 con­tain­ers of il­lic­it Car­ni­val brand cig­a­rettes, pur­chased in Ko­rea, ar­rived in Port-of-Spain, with the re­main­ing 20 await­ing con­fir­ma­tion.
The con­tain­ers were de­tained for ad­min­is­tra­tive is­sues.
“It was 32 con­tain­ers of to­bac­co. It was enor­mous, giv­en your pop­u­la­tion,” Ri­co said.
Each con­tain­er had 10 mil­lion cig­a­rettes, he said.
“We’re talk­ing about 320 mil­lion cig­a­rettes,” Ri­co said.
“The car­go was in the process of be­ing rerout­ed to Suri­name with the ul­ti­mate goal of be­ing smug­gled in­to Brazil, through the north­ern bor­der and a few to oth­er is­lands with­in the re­gion,” the re­port stat­ed.
The re­port showed a copy of the bill of lad­ing No. 6400908980, dat­ed No­vem­ber 27, 2025.
This date was is­sued ten months in ad­vance, in­di­cat­ing a clear pat­tern of fraud.
Fur­ther­more, the con­signee’s in­for­ma­tion was lat­er up­dat­ed on Feb­ru­ary 21, 2025, to an­oth­er lo­cal com­pa­ny, while the ship­ment was al­ready in tran­sit to Trinidad, prov­ing that smug­gled cig­a­rettes had en­tered the coun­try.
“In this method, bills of lad­ing and oth­er con­tain­er doc­u­men­ta­tion are al­tered to in­tro­duce false des­ti­na­tions and le­gal cov­ers, al­low­ing the car­go to be rerout­ed and dis­trib­uted to oth­er ports,” the re­port stat­ed.
One of the com­pa­nies iden­ti­fied in the re­port is close­ly linked to a Trinida­di­an busi­ness­man (name iden­ti­fied) who pur­chased Ko­re­an-brand cig­a­rettes.
The re­port stat­ed that the busi­ness­man main­tained per­son­al ties with a for­mer min­is­ter who re­port­ed­ly pro­tect­ed him.
The re­port fur­ther stat­ed that the busi­ness­man sought agree­ments with le­gal cig­a­rette op­er­a­tors, aim­ing to com­min­gle il­lic­it prod­ucts with le­gal ship­ments, us­ing au­tho­rised ware­hous­es.
“This ap­pears to be his new strat­e­gy fol­low­ing the re­vo­ca­tion of his Free Trade Zone li­cense. He has been on the radar since 2020, not as a re­sult of gov­ern­ment in­ves­ti­ga­tion, but due to in­tel­li­gence gath­ered by a pri­vate-sec­tor en­ti­ty.”
As of 2025, Ri­co said the Free Trade Zone frame­work had been re­placed by the Spe­cial Eco­nom­ic Zones (SEZ), aligned with Or­gan­i­sa­tion for Eco­nom­ic Co­op­er­a­tion and De­vel­op­ment guide­lines that strength­en reg­u­la­to­ry over­sight.
“All op­er­a­tors are now re­quired to reap­ply un­der this new sys­tem, which in­cludes height­ened com­pli­ance and reg­u­la­to­ry su­per­vi­sion.”
While the busi­ness holds a li­cence to im­port cig­a­rettes, it does not have au­tho­ri­sa­tion to bring them in­to the SEZ.
Based on the find­ings in the re­port, the busi­ness­man is one of three peo­ple in­volved in the smug­gling net­work.
“One was as­sas­si­nat­ed in Suri­name, and the oth­er fled to Brazil. These de­vel­op­ments sug­gest grow­ing in­ter­nal ten­sions and a reshuf­fling of roles with­in the il­lic­it trade net­works.”
Ac­cord­ing to the re­port, the busi­ness­man owes ap­prox­i­mate­ly US$500,000 in port stor­age fees.
“His mer­chan­dise was seized, and the con­tain­ers have been im­mo­bilised for over 30 months. To have them re­leased, he would need to pay this amount, which, com­pared to po­ten­tial il­lic­it prof­its, is con­sid­ered a min­i­mal penal­ty. Sit­u­a­tions like this re­veal how the cost of vi­o­lat­ing reg­u­la­tions can be in­signif­i­cant in com­par­i­son to the ben­e­fits of smug­gling.”
The plan is to pay the fees, reroute the con­tain­ers to Grena­da and then trans­fer them on­to food ves­sels to Suri­name.
There, the car­go will be con­sol­i­dat­ed on­to larg­er ves­sels for Belém in Brazil.
“We re­alised that T&T is used as a tran­ship­ment zone,” Ri­co said.
Since 2014, the US De­part­ment of State has iden­ti­fied Trinidad as a sig­nif­i­cant tran­ship­ment point for il­lic­it drugs.
“Il­lic­it to­bac­co works as a multi­na­tion­al crim­i­nal or­gan­i­sa­tion. So we would see pro­duc­ers in Paraguay and Ko­rea have been linked with cor­rup­tion, mon­ey laun­der­ing and nar­cotics. They pro­duced the cig­a­rettes in or­der to clean mon­ey. This is how ter­ror­ist or­gan­i­sa­tions prof­it from it,” Ri­co said.
More Lu­cra­tive than Nar­cotics
Big ship­ments al­so go to ter­ror­ist or­gan­i­sa­tions in Mex­i­co and Colom­bia.
Ri­co said it’s a prof­it-gen­er­at­ing busi­ness.
“It’s more lu­cra­tive than nar­cotics.”
He said the mon­ey flow from nar­cotics takes around six months to get back to the main sup­pli­er.
“With con­tra­band, this takes a month.”
Il­lic­it cig­a­rettes al­so en­ter the coun­try via pirogues and land in the hands of crim­i­nal gangs.
The re­port stat­ed that al­though there is no cur­rent dom­i­nance of street gangs in the cig­a­rette trade, “there is a grow­ing con­cern about the even­tu­al in­volve­ment of lo­cal crim­i­nal groups such as Ras­ta City (aka Sev­en), Mus­lim City (aka Sixx), and ABG (Any­body Gets It), or from for­eign gangs that al­so have a mi­nor pres­ence in the coun­try (cur­rent­ly these gangs are pri­mar­i­ly from Venezuela).”
In oth­er coun­tries, the re­port stat­ed that ter­ri­to­r­i­al con­trol by such groups quick­ly ex­tends to man­ag­ing the il­lic­it to­bac­co mar­ket.
“While vi­o­lence is not yet a defin­ing el­e­ment in this mar­ket, it would be a mis­take to as­sume this will re­main the case. These risks show the need for sus­tained mon­i­tor­ing and ear­ly in­ter­ven­tion mech­a­nisms to pre­vent an even­tu­al crim­i­nal con­sol­i­da­tion around the il­lic­it cig­a­rette trade.”
Il­lic­it cig­a­rettes al­so en­ter the coun­try us­ing pirogues that can car­ry up to 4,000 cas­es of cig­a­rettes, the re­port stat­ed.
Lu­cra­tive mar­ket
A pack of cig­a­rettes costs a lit­tle over US$0.20 to pro­duce, but can fetch be­tween US$2.22 and US$2.30 on the lo­cal mar­ket.
The West In­di­an To­bac­co Com­pa­ny Ltd (WIT­CO) man­u­fac­tures and mar­kets the Dun­hill, Lucky Strike and Roth­mans brands in Trinidad.
In a March 2026 ar­ti­cle, WIT­CO es­ti­mat­ed that il­lic­it cig­a­rette ac­tiv­i­ty had jumped 50 per cent since the 2026 ex­cise hike was an­nounced in last year’s bud­get.
Ex­cise du­ties on cig­a­rettes rose from $5.26 to $10.52 per 20-pack.
As a re­sult, WIT­CO raised the min­i­mum price for a pack of cig­a­rettes to $24.
Be­fore Ri­co’s ar­rival, the T&T Po­lice Ser­vice (TTPS) had al­ready launched an in­ves­ti­ga­tion in­to the theft of a ship­ment of IBIZA cig­a­rettes from the Port of Port-of-Spain in Oc­to­ber 2021.
The cig­a­rettes, which were not sub­ject to cus­toms pro­ce­dures, were stolen while in tran­sit to an­oth­er des­ti­na­tion.
This prompt­ed the po­lice to warn the pub­lic against buy­ing the pil­fered items.
The po­lice stat­ed that these items were not sub­ject to cus­toms pro­ce­dures.
Last Ju­ly, the To­bac­co Con­trol Unit un­der the Min­istry of Health gave a list of more than 50 un­li­censed/il­lic­it to­bac­co prod­ucts in T&T that should not be of­fered for sale, pur­chased by busi­ness­es or con­sumed by the pub­lic.
The list de­scribed the pack­ag­ing of cig­a­rettes, to­bac­co and cig­ars.
Among the il­lic­it cig­a­rettes iden­ti­fied were Car­ni­val, Gift, Sun­ny, Con­vay, Mil­lion­aire, Gold City and Black­stone.
Ri­co es­ti­mat­ed T&T’s cig­a­rette mar­ket at 1.2 bil­lion sticks.
The re­port re­vealed that the au­thor­i­ties be­gan to take is­sue with the il­le­gal cig­a­rette trade af­ter stolen cig­a­rette ship­ments were found stored in ho­tels.
A grow­ing con­cern in the re­port is the in­creas­ing in­volve­ment and role of the Chi­nese com­mu­ni­ty in cig­a­rette smug­gling and coun­ter­feit­ing op­er­a­tions.
“Au­thor­i­ties have iden­ti­fied an ex­pand­ing struc­ture op­er­at­ing with­out for­mal records or re­ceipts, and it is sus­pect­ed that the lead­ers of re­gion­al smug­gling op­er­a­tions are con­nect­ed to Chi­nese net­works,” the re­port stat­ed.
One emerg­ing pat­tern in the re­port in­volved some Chi­nese mer­chants im­port­ing their own brands of il­le­gal cig­a­rettes, pri­mar­i­ly in­tend­ed for con­sump­tion with­in their own com­mu­ni­ty.
“Ac­cord­ing to po­lice sources, these trans­ac­tions raised red flags as they are in­dica­tive of po­ten­tial mon­ey laun­der­ing schemes rather than sim­ple smug­gling,” the re­port stat­ed.
The au­thor­i­ties have in­ter­cept­ed ship­ments of cig­a­rettes in poor con­di­tion, linked to this com­pa­ny.
In 2021, the then Peo­ple’s Na­tion­al Move­ment gov­ern­ment, through a pub­lic/pri­vate part­ner­ship of or­gan­i­sa­tions, es­tab­lished an An­ti-Il­lic­it Trade Task Force (AIT­TF) to tack­le il­lic­it trade.
Among the 12 mem­bers on the task force are the Min­istry of Trade, Min­istry of Na­tion­al Se­cu­ri­ty, Cus­toms and Ex­cise Di­vi­sion, T&T Po­lice Ser­vice, Crime Stop­pers and the T&T Man­u­fac­tur­ers As­so­ci­a­tion (TTMA).
Be­tween 2021 and 2022, the po­lice’s Mul­ti-Agency Task Force and the To­bac­co Con­trol Unit seized 115,766 cig­a­rettes.
De­liv­er­ing the 2027 fis­cal pack­age last month, Fi­nance Min­is­ter Dav­en­dranath Tan­coo said the AIT­TF seized over 920,000 packs of il­le­gal cig­a­rettes be­tween June 2025 and Au­gust 2026, and promised to ac­cel­er­ate those ef­forts.
How­ev­er, the re­port stat­ed that the coun­try’s in­sti­tu­tion­al ca­pac­i­ty to in­ves­ti­gate and dis­man­tle or­gan­ised smug­gling net­works re­mains con­strained.
“Al­though oc­ca­sion­al seizures of cig­a­rettes oc­cur, these are not ac­com­pa­nied by thor­ough in­ves­ti­ga­tions aimed at un­cov­er­ing traf­fick­ing struc­tures, iden­ti­fy­ing key play­ers or ap­ply­ing le­gal tools such as as­set for­fei­ture.”
The re­port al­so stat­ed that penal­ties for smug­gling are es­sen­tial­ly ad­min­is­tra­tive.
“Al­though leg­is­la­tion such as the To­bac­co Act ex­ists which would al­low for crim­i­nal pros­e­cu­tion in prac­tice, it is not en­forced. In fact, it is re­port­ed that there are no in­di­vid­u­als im­pris­oned for smug­gling across the coun­try, ex­cept in ex­cep­tion­al cas­es of re­peat of­fences, such as when an in­di­vid­ual is caught three times,” the re­port stat­ed.
In 2015, Justin Mo­hammed was sen­tenced to 12 months in jail for throw­ing eight packs of cig­a­rettes over the wall of the Fred­er­ick Street Prison.
Sev­er­al prison of­fi­cers caught smug­gling cig­a­rettes in­to the prison were al­so ar­rest­ed and charged, with bare­ly any­one fac­ing jail time.
While T&T has been fight­ing il­le­gal to­bac­co, Ri­co said the au­thor­i­ties should leave no grey area for tran­ship­ment of con­tain­ers.
“Ban trans­ship­ments in the ports,” Ri­co said.
The re­port al­so stat­ed that mar­itime sur­veil­lance is lim­it­ed, with the smug­gling of il­le­gal cig­a­rettes over­looked.
Un­der the To­bac­co Con­trol Act, Chap­ter 30:04, no per­son shall man­u­fac­ture, im­port, ex­port or dis­trib­ute to­bac­co prod­ucts with­out a li­cence.
Al­so, no per­son shall sell or pur­chase any to­bac­co prod­uct from a man­u­fac­tur­er, dis­trib­u­tor, im­porter, ex­porter or whole­saler who is not li­censed un­der the Act.
On sum­ma­ry con­vic­tion, a per­son can face a $100,000 fine and six months’ im­pris­on­ment.
Up­on con­vic­tion on in­dict­ment, a per­son is li­able to a $200,000 fine and one year in prison.
The Sun­day Guardian sent a list of ques­tions to the TTMA, but the or­gan­i­sa­tion failed to re­spond.
Crime Stop­pers di­rec­tor Dar­rin Carmicheal said he was ad­vised not to speak on the is­sue.
Act­ing Com­mis­sion­er of Po­lice Ju­nior Ben­jamin was al­so sent a What­sApp mes­sage seek­ing in­for­ma­tion on the il­lic­it cig­a­rette trade, but there was no re­sponse.
WIT­CO bat­tles boom­ing il­le­gal cig­a­rette trade
Re­spond­ing to ques­tions by Guardian Me­dia, WIT­CO stat­ed that the il­le­gal cig­a­rette trade con­tin­ues to be a se­ri­ous eco­nom­ic, se­cu­ri­ty and reg­u­la­to­ry con­cern for the com­pa­ny.
“It de­prives the Gov­ern­ment of rev­enue, places le­git­i­mate man­u­fac­tur­ers and re­tail­ers at a com­pet­i­tive dis­ad­van­tage and cre­ates in­come for per­sons op­er­at­ing out­side the law.
“WIT­CO sup­ports bal­anced tax­a­tion to­geth­er with stronger, in­tel­li­gence-led en­force­ment, bor­der con­trols and col­lab­o­ra­tion among gov­ern­ment, law en­force­ment and le­git­i­mate in­dus­try.”
WIT­CO’s 2025 an­nu­al re­port es­ti­mat­ed that il­lic­it cig­a­rette ac­tiv­i­ty in­creased by 50 per cent fol­low­ing the ex­cise in­crease in last year’s bud­get
The ex­cise dou­bled from $5.26 to $10.52 per pack of 20.
More re­cent­ly, WIT­CO’s in­de­pen­dent in­dus­try and mar­ket re­search es­ti­mates a jump from eight to 15 per cent, ”al­most an 88 per cent in­crease in il­lic­it trade to date, at­trib­uted to the growth of the widen­ing price dif­fer­ence be­tween le­gal and il­le­gal prod­ucts.”
Es­ti­mates have shown the high prof­it mar­gins as­so­ci­at­ed with il­lic­it cig­a­rettes.
The com­pa­ny es­ti­mat­ed that a sin­gle con­tain­er of il­lic­it cig­a­rettes can gen­er­ate ap­prox­i­mate­ly US$1 mil­lion in prof­it.
The cost of a pack of il­le­gal cig­a­rettes ranged be­tween TT$10 and $15.
A le­gal pack is priced be­tween TT$20 and $24.
It said every il­le­gal pack sold dis­places a po­ten­tial le­git­i­mate sale while avoid­ing ex­cise du­ty, VAT, im­port du­ty, cor­po­ra­tion tax and oth­er fis­cal oblig­a­tions and reg­u­la­to­ry costs.
“This ad­verse­ly af­fects WIT­CO as well as le­git­i­mate dis­trib­u­tors, re­tail­ers, em­ploy­ees and the wider do­mes­tic man­u­fac­tur­ing val­ue chain.”
WIT­CO stat­ed that sev­er­al stud­ies and re­ports have shown that il­lic­it cig­a­rette trade fu­els transna­tion­al crime and gang ac­tiv­i­ty while un­der­min­ing brand in­tegri­ty.
“The broad­er crim­i­nal nexus is well recog­nised be­cause il­lic­it to­bac­co of­fers high po­ten­tial re­turns, is eas­i­ly trans­port­ed and may car­ry low­er per­ceived risks than oth­er forms of traf­fick­ing.”
Asked how this il­lic­it op­er­a­tion has af­fect­ed its busi­ness, WIT­CO stat­ed it cre­at­ed greater un­cer­tain­ty about in­vest­ment, dis­place­ment of le­gal sales, pres­sure on mar­ket share and brand val­ue, re­duced com­pet­i­tive­ness and even in­creased op­er­a­tional ex­pen­di­ture.
WIT­CO ad­mit­ted that the il­le­gal trade has placed sig­nif­i­cant pres­sure on its vol­umes, com­pet­i­tive­ness and prof­itabil­i­ty.
“We have had to make in­vest­ments in a brand which can be sold at a price to com­pete with the large price gap cre­at­ed by the ex­cise in­crease be­tween le­gal and il­le­gal, so while our vol­umes may have in­creased since then, the val­ue pool con­tin­ues to be erod­ed.”
A look at WIT­CO’s an­nu­al re­port showed that prof­it de­clined from 2023 to the cur­rent.
It dropped from 65 per cent to 48 per cent.
WIT­CO said that, based on pub­licly avail­able ship­ping da­ta, most of the il­le­gal cig­a­rettes are com­ing via Pana­ma.
WIT­CO iden­ti­fied one brand called Car­ni­val, which has a high pres­ence on the il­le­gal cig­a­rettes mar­ket, made by KT&G (Ko­re­an To­bac­co and Gin­seng).
The com­pa­ny be­lieves that “15 per cent of the mar­ket en­ters as il­le­gal an­nu­al­ly.”
It added il­le­gal cig­a­rettes have been seen in small gro­ceries and ped­dled by street ven­dors.
As such WIT­CO has called for a mul­ti-pronged ap­proach to deal with the il­lic­it mar­ket.
“Stronger and more con­sis­tent en­force­ment is need­ed. But it should fo­cus on dis­rupt­ing sup­ply and dis­tri­b­u­tion net­works…not on­ly on seizures at the re­tail lev­el. The em­pha­sis should be on dis­man­tling the fi­nan­cial, im­por­ta­tion, stor­age and dis­tri­b­u­tion net­works be­hind the trade.”

Prime Min­is­ter Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar is en­cour­ag­ing unions to set aside their “ha­tred” and put their mem­bers first by seek­ing di­a­logue with the Gov­ern­ment.
In a Face­book post yes­ter­day, a day af­ter sev­er­al trade unions staged a march in Port-of-Spain, the Prime Min­is­ter dou­bled down on her as­sess­ment of the march, say­ing, “Fol­low­ing the spec­tac­u­lar­ly failed protest yes­ter­day, which at­tract­ed at its peak about 400 peo­ple dri­ven by po­lit­i­cal and racial ha­tred of the UNC, the gov­ern­ment en­cour­ages those unions to set aside their ha­tred and put their mem­bers first.”
“The pop­u­la­tion has re­ject­ed their di­vi­sive rhetoric and there­fore I call on them to put aside their per­son­al in­ter­ests, bias, and ha­tred and work with the gov­ern­ment as oth­er unions are do­ing to set­tle ne­go­ti­a­tions in a re­spon­si­ble man­ner,” she added.
She not­ed that her Gov­ern­ment had re­cent­ly set­tled pro­tract­ed wage ne­go­ti­a­tions for Pow­er­Gen work­ers.
“Yes­ter­day, while a small group of mis­guid­ed peo­ple and a hun­dred thou­sand ghosts were march­ing against the UNC, the Min­is­ter of Pub­lic Util­i­ties made an an­nounce­ment in the Par­lia­ment of a $66.1 mil­lion set­tle­ment with the Oil­field Work­ers’ Trade Union (OW­TU),” Per­sad-Bisses­sar said.
How­ev­er, Sea­men and Wa­ter­front Work­ers Trade Union (SWW­TU) pres­i­dent Michael An­nisette has dis­missed crit­i­cism over a per­ceived low turnout at a labour move­ment ral­ly in Port-of-Spain on Fri­day.
In a tele­phone in­ter­view yes­ter­day, An­nisette, who al­so serves as gen­er­al sec­re­tary of the Na­tion­al Trade Union Cen­tre (NATUC), hailed the event as a suc­cess de­spite ad­mit­ting that it at­tract­ed few­er par­tic­i­pants than sim­i­lar ac­tion in the past.
An­nisette said: “Maybe they were ex­pect­ing 10,000 or 15,000. No, we did not have that. I will read­i­ly ad­mit it. But in the cir­cum­stances, one has to be sat­is­fied with the march that came out.”
The vet­er­an trade union­ist claimed that the num­ber of par­tic­i­pants in the protest is not the on­ly met­ric that can be used to mea­sure its suc­cess.
“It’s not about num­bers. It’s about com­mit­ment. It’s about peo­ple who are will­ing to come out and act,” An­nisette said.
Stat­ing that the march at­tract­ed thou­sands, in­clud­ing many who sup­port­ed from van­tage points along the route, An­nisette claimed that de­trac­tors sought to utilise area still pho­tographs of seg­ments of the march in or­der to claim that on­ly hun­dreds par­tic­i­pat­ed.
“They nev­er showed the to­tal march, the length of the march and the peo­ple that were in­volved from all the dif­fer­ent unions,” he said.
An­nisette al­so re­ject­ed crit­i­cism from Prime Min­is­ter Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar, who ques­tioned the tim­ing of the march while claim­ing that sim­i­lar ac­tion was not tak­en by the trade union move­ment un­der the Peo­ple’s Na­tion­al Move­ment (PNM) ad­min­is­tra­tion be­tween 2015 and 2025.
He not­ed that NATUC held a ma­jor march in 2022.
An­nisette al­so chal­lenged claims that the trade unions politi­cised the march by al­low­ing PNM par­lia­men­tar­i­ans and of­fi­cials to par­tic­i­pate.
He said that trade unions must en­gage politi­cians, as laws and poli­cies that af­fect cit­i­zens, in­clud­ing their mem­bers, are shaped by them (politi­cians).
“It is not about pol­i­tics. It is about the eco­nom­ic re­al­i­ties and the so­cio-eco­nom­ic is­sues that work­ers have to face day to day,” he added.
He not­ed that trade unions al­so have a re­spon­si­bil­i­ty to raise so­cio-eco­nom­ic con­cerns af­fect­ing cit­i­zens and are not con­fined to ne­go­ti­at­ing over their mem­bers’ terms and con­di­tions of em­ploy­ment.
“We rep­re­sent the voice­less, the dis­ad­van­taged com­mu­ni­ties, the sin­gle par­ents and their chil­dren, who may not get three square meals a day be­cause of the salaries of their moth­er or fa­ther,” An­nisette said.
Con­tact­ed yes­ter­day, po­lit­i­cal sci­en­tist Dr Bish­nu Ra­goonath said that the per­ceived low turnout might be due to the politi­ci­sa­tion of the event.
“What start­ed off prob­a­bly as a good think­ing union protest was al­lowed to gen­er­ate in­to a po­lit­i­cal march. I think that will give the Unit­ed Na­tion­al Con­gress (UNC) some de­gree of com­fort to say that this was not strict­ly a trade union protest against them, but rather it was a po­lit­i­cal protest,” Ra­goonath said.
He claimed that the lack of de­mar­ca­tion over the true in­tent of the event may have led to some trade unions and their mem­bers stay­ing away to avoid march­ing along­side for­mer gov­ern­ment of­fi­cials who they protest­ed against in the past.
Po­lit­i­cal an­a­lyst Dr Win­ford James said that he did not close­ly fol­low the ral­ly.
James al­so ques­tioned the per­ceived low par­tic­i­pa­tion of PNM mem­bers de­spite the at­ten­dance of se­nior par­ty of­fi­cials.
“The Op­po­si­tion sup­port did not seem to be some­thing the PNM could gloat about,” James said.

Trinidad and To­ba­go’s Gov­ern­ment came in for praise on so­cial me­dia site X, for­mer­ly Twit­ter, from Unit­ed States Deputy Sec­re­tary of State Christo­pher Lan­dau on Fri­day night for vot­ing with the US against re­mov­ing its em­bar­go on Cu­ba.
Lan­dau re­spond­ed to a post from Prime Min­is­ter Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar on her Gov­ern­ment’s rea­son for vot­ing against the an­nu­al Unit­ed Na­tions res­o­lu­tion call­ing for an end to the US eco­nom­ic, com­mer­cial and fi­nan­cial em­bar­go on Cu­ba.
The res­o­lu­tion was passed, with 130 in favour, 17 against and 25 ab­sten­tions.
Trinidad and To­ba­go was the on­ly Cari­com coun­try to vote “No.” A num­ber of Cari­com coun­tries, in­clud­ing Ja­maica and Guyana, were among those to ab­stain.
On Oc­to­ber 28, Per­sad-Bisses­sar post­ed a state­ment on X de­fend­ing the Gov­ern­ment’s vote, which rep­re­sents a shift in pol­i­cy af­ter decades of sup­port­ing the UN res­o­lu­tion.
She said the coun­try’s vote re­flect­ed the Gov­ern­ment’s “firm and un­wa­ver­ing com­mit­ment to democ­ra­cy, free­dom and fun­da­men­tal rights of all peo­ple.”
Per­sad-Bisses­sar said she has made it clear that T&T will not sup­port mil­i­tary dic­ta­tor­ship in Cu­ba. She said the US gov­ern­ment has been spear­head­ing a cam­paign for democ­ra­cy in Cu­ba and men­tioned Sec­re­tary of State Mar­co Ru­bio’s com­ments that there must be po­lit­i­cal re­forms in Cu­ba.
In re­sponse late on Oc­to­ber 30, Lan­dau said, “Prime Min­is­ter, the US recog­nis­es and thanks your gov­ern­ment for vot­ing in favour of a de­mo­c­ra­t­ic tran­si­tion in Cu­ba at the UN this year.”
He said the US was proud to stand along­side T&T and oth­er democ­ra­cies in the re­gion to call out the “re­pres­sive” Cuban regime.
“How can coun­tries vote in favour of a regime that has not al­lowed its own peo­ple to vote for al­most 68 YEARS?! May God bless you and the peo­ple of your love­ly coun­try, which I was proud to vis­it a few months ago,” Lan­dau added.
Per­sad-Bisses­sar replied, thank­ing Lan­dau.
“The Gov­ern­ment of Trinidad and To­ba­go stands for democ­ra­cy, free­dom, hu­man dig­ni­ty and the right of every cit­i­zen, in­clud­ing the peo­ple of Cu­ba, to freely de­ter­mine their po­lit­i­cal fu­ture,” she added.
It is not the first time Lan­dau, on be­half of the US, has heaped praise on Per­sad-Bisses­sar and her Gov­ern­ment.  In Sep­tem­ber 2025, the US State De­part­ment re­leased de­tails of a call be­tween the US Deputy Sec­re­tary of State and Prime Min­is­ter Per­sad-Bisses­sar.
Ac­cord­ing to the state­ment, Lan­dau reaf­firmed the strength of the US–Trinidad and To­ba­go part­ner­ship, de­scrib­ing the coun­try as a “strong US part­ner in the Caribbean.”
He ac­knowl­edged the Prime Min­is­ter’s pub­lic sup­port of US mil­i­tary op­er­a­tions in the South Caribbean Sea and em­pha­sised both gov­ern­ments’ com­mit­ment to com­bat­ing il­le­gal nar­cotics and firearms traf­fick­ing. The Deputy Sec­re­tary al­so high­light­ed the im­por­tance of es­tab­lish­ing a UN Sup­port Of­fice for Haiti, with both lead­ers stress­ing the need for in­ter­na­tion­al as­sis­tance to ad­dress in­se­cu­ri­ty and vi­o­lence there.
He met the Prime Min­is­ter face-to-face in Au­gust this year.
Browne: Shame on
Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar
But de­spite the praise from the US, For­mer for­eign af­fairs min­is­ter Dr Amery Browne has heav­i­ly crit­i­cised the Gov­ern­ment for its stance at the UN.
Re­spond­ing to Guardian Me­dia yes­ter­day, Browne said the vote has “re­al­ly tar­nished our na­tion and dis­graced our for­eign ser­vice.”
Browne said the Prime Min­is­ter and her regime have placed T&T on the wrong side of his­to­ry and against the UN char­ter.
“With that dis­grace­ful mi­nor­i­ty vote this past week to sup­port the star­va­tion and the siege of the peo­ple of Cu­ba, our coun­try is con­firmed as a vas­sal state whose sov­er­eign voice has been sold out and whose stan­dards have been farmed out,” Browne said.
He said Trin­bag­o­ni­ans are gen­er­ous peo­ple with com­pas­sion and warm hearts.
“Sad­ly, we are bur­dened with the most un­prin­ci­pled and heart­less prime min­is­ter and a regime that en­dors­es the star­va­tion of mil­lions of in­no­cent Cubans, in­clud­ing chil­dren. “The UNC has re­ject­ed the zone of peace, but it em­braces geno­cide, the mass de­pri­va­tion of food, and the use of black­outs as a po­lit­i­cal weapon. Shame on Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar.”

A man from Laven­tille has been sen­tenced to hang for mur­der­ing a 16-year-old boy fol­low­ing an al­ter­ca­tion in 2009.
Jus­tice Maria Bus­by-Ear­le-Cad­dle read the manda­to­ry death sen­tence for Sim­ba Dick­son af­ter he was found guilty by a 12-mem­ber ju­ry at the Hall of Jus­tice in Port-of-Spain, ear­li­er this week.
Dick­son, of St Barbs, Laven­tille, was ac­cused of mur­der­ing De­von Blake on Feb­ru­ary 8, 2009.
Dick­son re­port­ed­ly had an ar­gu­ment with Blake while they were both walk­ing along a road in Bel­mont.
Res­i­dents saw Dick­son slap Blake be­fore they in­ter­vened to sep­a­rate the two.
Lat­er that evening, Dick­son re­port­ed­ly went to the teenag­er's house and asked for him to come out­side.
Blake's rel­a­tives told him he was not home and he left. They claimed they saw a gun in Dick­son's back-pock­et as he was walk­ing away.
Lat­er that night, Blake was shot in his back while lim­ing in the front gallery of his home.
He was tak­en to the hos­pi­tal but died while re­ceiv­ing treat­ment.
Al­though no one saw Dick­son shoot­ing Blake, Blake's rel­a­tives and neigh­bours claimed that they saw him (Dick­son) run­ning away af­ter hear­ing the gun­shot.
Dick­son chose to not tes­ti­fy in his de­fence but called his sis­ter as a wit­ness as she claimed that he was at her house at the time of the shoot­ing.
How­ev­er, As­sis­tant Di­rec­tor of Pub­lic Pros­e­cu­tions (DPP) Dy­lan Mar­tin dis­cred­it­ed the claimed al­i­bi while in­tense­ly in­ter­ro­gat­ing her.
While un­der cross-ex­am­i­na­tion, she ad­mit­ted that Dick­son briefly left her house to go to a par­lour.
She ad­mit­ted that she could not see the par­lour from her house and could not con­clu­sive­ly say if Dick­son was there at the rel­e­vant time.
Mar­tin al­so point­ed out that Dick­son ini­tial­ly told the po­lice he was at an­oth­er lo­ca­tion at the time of the mur­der and not at her house. Dick­son's sis­ter ac­knowl­edged the dis­crep­an­cy.
She even­tu­al­ly con­fessed that her claims over her broth­er's where­abouts were fab­ri­cat­ed.
The ju­rors took just over one and a half hours to de­lib­er­ate be­fore unan­i­mous­ly find­ing that Dick­son was guilty be­yond a rea­son­able doubt.

The de­lay in ap­point­ing five new Court of Ap­peal judges is rais­ing con­cerns in the le­gal fra­ter­ni­ty as three sit­ting ap­pel­late judges pre­pare to demit of­fice, cre­at­ing un­cer­tain­ty over the arrange­ments for No­vem­ber.
A se­nior ju­di­cial of­fi­cer told Guardian Me­dia that the Ju­di­cial and Le­gal Ser­vice Com­mis­sion (JLSC) sub­mit­ted its rec­om­men­da­tions for the five ap­point­ments to Pres­i­dent Chris­tine Kan­ga­loo last Wednes­day.
How­ev­er, as of yes­ter­day, the in­stru­ments of ap­point­ment had still not been is­sued by Pres­i­dent’s House. Jus­tice of Ap­peal Prakash Moo­sai has re­tired fol­low­ing al­most three decades on the Bench, while the tem­po­rary ap­pel­late ap­point­ments of Jus­tices Car­ol Gob­in and Joan Charles are al­so com­ing to an end, with both judges ex­pect­ed to re­turn to the High Court.
Fol­low­ing their de­par­tures, the Court of Ap­peal is ex­pect­ed to have on­ly 11 of its au­tho­rised com­ple­ment of 16 judges, leav­ing five po­si­tions va­cant.
The source said the de­lay comes as the Ju­di­cia­ry has al­ready pre­pared its No­vem­ber hear­ing al­lo­ca­tions in an­tic­i­pa­tion of the five new ap­point­ments. Ori­en­ta­tion meet­ings had al­so been arranged to fa­cil­i­tate the in­com­ing judges’ com­mence­ment of sit­tings from No­vem­ber 6, but Guardian Me­dia un­der­stands that those arrange­ments have been placed on hold be­cause the ap­point­ment in­stru­ments re­main out­stand­ing. A re­li­able source with­in the le­gal fra­ter­ni­ty warned that fail­ure to com­plete the ap­point­ments could af­fect the con­sti­tu­tion of ap­pel­late pan­els, force the re­al­lo­ca­tion or post­pone­ment of sched­uled ap­peals and re­sult in fur­ther de­lays for lit­i­gants await­ing the de­ter­mi­na­tion of their cas­es.
In re­sponse to Guardian Me­dia, how­ev­er, the Of­fice of the Pres­i­dent as­sured that what­ev­er con­sti­tu­tion­al arrange­ments need­ed to be done would be done.
“The Of­fice of the Pres­i­dent wish­es to ad­vise that all con­cerned can rest as­sured that as­sum­ing any arrange­ments are re­quired to be made, any arrange­ments that might be re­quired to be made, will so be made, in the due and prop­er dis­charge by this of­fice of what­ev­er Con­sti­tu­tion­al arrange­ments might re­quire to be made.”
Pri­or to this re­sponse, the ju­di­cial source raised con­sti­tu­tion­al con­cerns about the de­lay, point­ing to Sec­tion 104(1) of the Con­sti­tu­tion, which pro­vides that judges, oth­er than the Chief Jus­tice, are ap­point­ed by the Pres­i­dent act­ing in ac­cor­dance with the ad­vice of the JLSC.
The source sub­mit­ted that the Pres­i­dent is en­trust­ed with im­por­tant con­sti­tu­tion­al re­spon­si­bil­i­ties, but the ex­er­cise of those re­spon­si­bil­i­ties must re­main with­in the lim­its and oblig­a­tions pre­scribed by the Con­sti­tu­tion.

eliz­a­beth.gon­za­les@guardian.co.tt
In the last year, sev­er­al state bod­ies have been found to be in breach of the pro­cure­ment law, po­ten­tial­ly cost­ing tax­pay­ers al­most $166,000 in le­gal fees. These in­clude three ten­der eval­u­a­tion fail­ures sim­i­lar to those un­cov­ered in the Hous­ing De­vel­op­ment Cor­po­ra­tion’s (HDC) can­celled $3.48 bil­lion hous­ing pro­gramme.
The find­ings in­volve the Min­istry of Trans­port and Civ­il Avi­a­tion, Trinidad and To­ba­go Elec­tric­i­ty Com­mis­sion (T&TEC), Paria Fu­el Trad­ing and the To­ba­go Re­gion­al Health Au­thor­i­ty (TRHA). All four lost pro­cure­ment chal­lenges be­fore hear­ing pan­els ap­point­ed by the Of­fice of Pro­cure­ment Reg­u­la­tion (OPR).
In the OPR de­ci­sion doc­u­ments, Guardian Me­dia found that the pan­els or­dered the pub­lic bod­ies to pay a com­bined $165,920.83 in le­gal costs to con­trac­tors who chal­lenged their ten­der de­ci­sions - those are costs award­ed by the reg­u­la­tor, not fines.
One OPR pan­el put the rule at the cen­tre of these cas­es in plain terms: “It was not open for a pub­lic body to se­lect a ten­der­er by a dif­fer­ent method­ol­o­gy.”
That warn­ing was is­sued in a case in­volv­ing ve­hi­cle in­spec­tion stick­ers, not hous­ing. But the rule is the same one cit­ed in the in­quiry in­to HDC’s pro­posed hous­ing con­tracts. In three of the four de­ci­sions, the reg­u­la­tor found that the pub­lic body had failed to fol­low the eval­u­a­tion method dis­closed to bid­ders.
The fourth de­ci­sion, de­liv­ered against the TRHA on Oc­to­ber 16, found breach­es of two pro­vi­sions of the Pro­cure­ment Act. Its pub­lished or­der does not set out full writ­ten rea­sons, so the pre­cise na­ture of those fail­ures can­not yet be com­pared with HDC’s.
What the HDC re­port found
The lat­est rul­ings came af­ter Guardian Me­dia re­port­ed on Oc­to­ber 18 the OPR’s de­tailed find­ings con­cern­ing HDC’s $3.48 bil­lion hous­ing pro­gramme. The pro­posed pro­cure­ment cov­ered 11 pack­ages of build­ing and in­fra­struc­ture work at hous­ing de­vel­op­ments across Trinidad.
Un­der the De­sign-Build-Fi­nance mod­el, con­trac­tors were ex­pect­ed to arrange fi­nanc­ing for the work. The OPR ex­am­ined how HDC in­vit­ed bids, checked the ca­pac­i­ty of con­trac­tors and ar­rived at its rec­om­men­da­tions for award.
The in­quiry found that HDC had asked bid­ders for three years of au­dit­ed fi­nan­cial state­ments but had not set out a scor­ing method or min­i­mum stan­dard to test whether they could fi­nance the projects. The re­port said there was no ev­i­dence that those state­ments had been as­sessed to es­tab­lish bid­ders’ fi­nan­cial ca­pac­i­ty.
It al­so found prob­lems with the eval­u­a­tion of manda­to­ry re­quire­ments and changes in how some cri­te­ria were ap­plied. In one case, a bid­der’s tech­ni­cal score rose from 36.93 to 76.03 af­ter a re-eval­u­a­tion on April 7. The bid­der moved from tech­ni­cal­ly non-com­pli­ant to be­ing rec­om­mend­ed for award.
The cor­po­ra­tion can­celled the pro­cure­ment on June 17, 2026. The OPR’s in­quiry re­port was dat­ed Ju­ly 1. The $3.48 bil­lion was the stat­ed val­ue of the pro­posed pack­ages. It was not a find­ing that this amount had been paid out.
The OPR sub­se­quent­ly opened a sep­a­rate in­ves­ti­ga­tion in­to al­le­ga­tions con­cern­ing the HDC process. The OPR con­firmed on Oc­to­ber 8 that its sep­a­rate probe in­to al­le­ga­tions of bid rig­ging and col­lu­sion was on­go­ing.
Price left out of Trans­port de­ci­sion
A pro­cure­ment for ve­hi­cle in­spec­tion stick­ers ex­posed one of the clear­est ex­am­ples of how eval­u­a­tion rules may have been dis­re­gard­ed.
In June 2026, the Min­istry of Trans­port and Civ­il Avi­a­tion sought bids for the sup­ply and de­liv­ery of se­cure in­spec­tion stick­ers and print­ing con­sum­ables over three years. Four com­pa­nies sub­mit­ted bids.
The ten­der stat­ed that tech­ni­cal qual­i­ty would car­ry 70 per cent of the score and the price would car­ry 30 per cent. It al­so showed how those scores should be cal­cu­lat­ed and com­bined.
JAB­CO Lim­it­ed of­fered the low­est price, ap­prox­i­mate­ly 48 per cent be­low that of Pow­er Cy­cle Lim­it­ed, which the min­istry rec­om­mend­ed for the con­tract. JAB­CO chal­lenged the de­ci­sion.
The OPR found that the min­istry’s eval­u­a­tion com­mit­tee had cho­sen the bid­der with the high­est tech­ni­cal score with­out cal­cu­lat­ing the re­quired com­bined score. In do­ing so, it left out the 30 per cent fi­nan­cial com­po­nent.
The hear­ing pan­el did not find that JAB­CO should nec­es­sar­i­ly have won the con­tract. Its de­ci­sion was that the min­istry had not fol­lowed the rules set out in its own ten­der doc­u­ments.
On Sep­tem­ber 9, the reg­u­la­tor or­dered the min­istry to ter­mi­nate the pro­cure­ment and pay JAB­CO $43,100 in le­gal costs. Writ­ten rea­sons fol­lowed on Oc­to­ber 9.
Con­fi­den­tial terms in T&TEC ten­der
T&TEC faced a sim­i­lar find­ing over a ten­der to up­grade the first phase of its IP video sur­veil­lance sys­tem.
Jian En­ter­pris­es Lim­it­ed chal­lenged the re-eval­u­a­tion of bids af­ter KVR En­er­gy Lim­it­ed was iden­ti­fied as the pro­posed suc­cess­ful bid­der. The dis­pute fol­lowed an ear­li­er chal­lenge and a con­fi­den­tial sched­ule of agreed terms be­tween the par­ties.
The new eval­u­a­tion used a method un­der which bid­ders could re­ceive full marks for a cri­te­ri­on un­less a spe­cif­ic fail­ure was iden­ti­fied. The method was not in the orig­i­nal ten­der doc­u­ments.
The OPR pan­el found that a pri­vate agree­ment could not change a State body’s du­ty to eval­u­ate all ten­ders ac­cord­ing to the pub­lished rules. As the writ­ten rea­sons stat­ed: “A pri­vate agree­ment be­tween the procur­ing en­ti­ty and a bid­der could not al­ter that re­quire­ment.”
The de­ci­sion al­so record­ed that Jian’s bid was ap­prox­i­mate­ly 14.2 per cent low­er than KVR’s, but both re­ceived full marks for price. The pan­el made clear that iden­ti­cal price scores were not, on their own, proof of a breach. The un­law­ful step was the use of an undis­closed eval­u­a­tion method.
The pan­el or­dered T&TEC to ter­mi­nate the pro­cure­ment on Au­gust 14 and pay Jian $42,337.50 in costs. Its writ­ten rea­sons said there was in­suf­fi­cient ev­i­dence to es­tab­lish the chal­lenger’s al­le­ga­tions of bias or a de­lib­er­ate at­tempt to favour KVR.
A pric­ing test bid­ders did not know
At Paria Fu­el Trad­ing, the dis­put­ed pro­cure­ment was for ma­rine se­cu­ri­ty ser­vices.
The com­pa­ny is­sued a fresh in­vi­ta­tion to bid in Oc­to­ber 2025, af­ter can­celling an ear­li­er ex­er­cise. Bid­ders were told their prices would be as­sessed against in­dus­try stan­dards.
But Paria’s eval­u­a­tors used an in­ter­nal com­pa­ny es­ti­mate and undis­closed price bands. Bids clos­er to that es­ti­mate re­ceived high­er scores. Amal­ga­mat­ed Se­cu­ri­ty Ser­vices Lim­it­ed chal­lenged the process.
The OPR found that Paria had used a method bid­ders could not have known from the ten­der doc­u­ments. The pan­el said the undis­closed sys­tem made the com­mer­cial eval­u­a­tion “pro­ce­du­ral­ly un­fair and legal­ly in­valid”.
Paria can­celled the pro­cure­ment on March 27 this year, af­ter the chal­lenge was filed. But the pan­el ruled that can­cel­la­tion did not erase the bid­der’s right to seek le­gal costs if a breach had oc­curred.
The April 28 or­der re­quired Paria to pay Amal­ga­mat­ed Se­cu­ri­ty Ser­vices $36,383.33, rep­re­sent­ing one-third of as­sessed le­gal costs. The writ­ten rea­sons were is­sued in May.
Lat­est rul­ing in To­ba­go
The most re­cent de­ci­sion con­cerns the TRHA’s ten­der for con­sul­tan­cy ser­vices to im­ple­ment a qual­i­ty man­age­ment sys­tem.
J.M. Mer­cedes Prop­er­ty Man­age­ment, Con­sul­tan­cy and Con­tract­ing Ser­vices Lim­it­ed brought the chal­lenge. In an or­der dat­ed Oc­to­ber 16, the OPR found that the au­thor­i­ty breached Sec­tions 5(2) and 30(1)(a) of the Act.
The hear­ing pan­el or­dered the TRHA to pay the com­pa­ny $44,100 in le­gal costs by De­cem­ber 16. It dis­missed a sep­a­rate claim for the bid­der’s sub­mis­sion costs be­cause that amount had not been proved.
Un­like the three oth­er cas­es, the OPR’s pub­lic reg­is­ter did not con­tain de­tailed writ­ten rea­sons for the TRHA rul­ing. It would there­fore be wrong to say the same eval­u­a­tion-method breach was es­tab­lished in that case.
Changes to the law
There is an­oth­er is­sue fol­low­ing the HDC re­port. On Oc­to­ber 9, the Gov­ern­ment’s amend­ments to the pro­cure­ment law were sub­se­quent­ly pub­lished as an Act of Par­lia­ment, ef­fec­tive­ly chang­ing what the OPR can do af­ter cer­tain com­plaints and in­ves­ti­ga­tions.
Un­der the amend­ed Sec­tion 44, the reg­u­la­tor can­not use a Part IV com­plaint or in­ves­ti­ga­tion to or­der a pub­lic body to sus­pend a ten­der, re-eval­u­ate bids, over­turn a con­tract or ter­mi­nate pro­cure­ment pro­ceed­ings. Rec­om­men­da­tions made un­der that Part are ad­vi­so­ry and not bind­ing.
The changes al­so ex­empt qual­i­fy­ing pub­lic-pri­vate part­ner­ships for pub­lic hous­ing from the Act’s pro­cure­ment re­quire­ments.
That has im­pli­ca­tions for any fu­ture de­ci­sion to re­tender HDC’s hous­ing pack­ages.
An OPR source said the find­ings against HDC were sup­port­ed by the rules gov­ern­ing pub­lic pro­cure­ment. But the source al­so raised con­cerns about what the re­cent amend­ment means for fu­ture hous­ing con­tracts.
When asked whether the on­go­ing HDC in­ves­ti­ga­tion was now ef­fec­tive­ly a waste fol­low­ing the pro­cure­ment amend­ments, the source replied:
“Well, ba­si­cal­ly, yes. It could on­ly be based on the amend­ment to the Act.”
How­ev­er, the source said the au­dit was well ex­e­cut­ed. “And I think based on the find­ings and the con­clu­sion, it was a well done au­dit in­ves­ti­ga­tion on the cir­cum­stances un­der which these things were award­ed.”
The source said that if the can­celled HDC hous­ing pack­ages are put out to ten­der again un­der a pub­lic-hous­ing pub­lic-pri­vate part­ner­ship, the new ex­emp­tion could put those con­tracts out­side the OPR’s nor­mal pro­cure­ment over­sight.
The source de­scribed the po­si­tion con­fronting the reg­u­la­tor in stark terms.
“They are be­tween a rock and a hard place. That’s the OPR in terms of what they can do and what they can’t do.”
The source said the changes would not pre­vent a sep­a­rate crim­i­nal in­ves­ti­ga­tion if ev­i­dence of wrong­do­ing emerged.
“That doesn’t stop the DPP or the po­lice from con­duct­ing an in­ves­ti­ga­tion if there is any al­leged cor­rup­tion or cor­rupt prac­tices.”
The source said the amend­ments do not ter­mi­nate in­ves­ti­ga­tions that be­gan be­fore the law changed.
Ef­forts to con­tact Reg­u­la­tor Bev­er­ly Khan were un­suc­cess­ful.

In re­cent weeks, this coun­try’s his­toric build­ings have come in­to sharp fo­cus af­ter the Gov­ern­ment said White­hall re­quired sub­stan­tial re­fur­bish­ment and it did not have the funds to do so at the mo­ment.
But while much of the dis­cus­sion has cen­tred around pol­i­tics, his­to­ry buffs or those fas­ci­nat­ed with build­ings like the Mag­nif­i­cent Sev­en have been lob­by­ing for these places to be cher­ished, re­fur­bished and pre­served. His­to­ry en­thu­si­ast Pa­tri­cia Bisses­sar be­lieves us­ing White­hall as an ad­min­is­tra­tive of­fice has con­tributed to its di­lap­i­da­tion over the years.
In an in­ter­view with Guardian Me­dia last week, Bisses­sar ad­vo­cat­ed for White­hall and the oth­er build­ings that make up the Mag­nif­i­cent Sev­en — Mille Fleurs, Queen’s Roy­al Col­lege, Stollmey­er’s Cas­tle, Arch­bish­op’s House, Roomor and Hayes Court — to be­come tourist at­trac­tions.
Of the sev­en, White­hall, Mille Fleurs, QRC and Stollmey­er’s Cas­tle are state-owned while the oth­ers are pri­vate­ly owned.
White­hall, orig­i­nal­ly called Rosen­weg, was built along Mar­aval Road in 1904 by a wealthy co­coa planter named Joseph Leon Agos­ti­ni.
Us­ing im­port­ed white coral from Bar­ba­dos and de­signed in a Moor­ish Mediter­ranean style with in­flu­ences from the ar­chi­tec­ture of Cor­si­ca, where Agos­ti­ni’s fam­i­ly orig­i­nat­ed, the con­struc­tion took three years.
Af­ter Agos­ti­ni’s death in 1906, ac­cord­ing to the Na­tion­al Trust, his fam­i­ly re­mained in res­i­dence un­til 1910, when the prop­er­ty was fore­closed for lack of mort­gage pay­ments.
It was sold to an Amer­i­can busi­ness­man from Venezuela named Robert Hen­der­son.
The Na­tion­al Trust said dur­ing Hen­der­son’s own­er­ship, a “de­light­ful va­ri­ety of fur­nish­ings of the in­te­ri­or was added to the re­fined dig­ni­ty of the ex­te­ri­or.”
The Hen­der­son fam­i­ly al­so re­named it White Hall, af­ter the coral stone used in con­struc­tion.
The build­ing was com­man­deered from Hen­der­son’s heirs dur­ing the Sec­ond World War as head­quar­ters of the Air Raid Pre­cau­tion.
In 1944, it was rent­ed by the British Coun­cil as a cul­tur­al cen­tre and lat­er, the Trinidad Cen­tral Li­brary, Re­gion­al Li­brary, Na­tion­al Archive, Gov­ern­ment Broad­cast­ing Unit, Trinidad Art So­ci­ety and the Cel­lar Club all oc­cu­pied space in the build­ing.
Five years lat­er, the build­ing stood emp­ty un­til 1954 when it was pur­chased by the Gov­ern­ment.
In 1963, af­ter In­de­pen­dence, it be­came the Of­fice of the Prime Min­is­ter, oc­cu­pied by the coun­try’s first prime min­is­ter Dr Er­ic Williams.
In 2000, White­hall was re­stored and con­tin­ued to be used as the OPM.
In 2009, it was evac­u­at­ed due to an ad­vanced state of di­lap­i­da­tion.
In 2016, a ma­jor restora­tion start­ed, with de­sign­ers in­te­grat­ing mod­ern con­ve­niences “with­out com­pro­mis­ing the in­te­ri­or or ex­te­ri­or fin­ish­es,” the Na­tion­al Trust said. Bud­get records showed the restora­tion and out­fit­ting were com­plet­ed at a cost of $32 mil­lion, al­low­ing the Of­fice of the Prime Min­is­ter to re-oc­cu­py White­hall in Sep­tem­ber 2019 af­ter a ten-year ab­sence.
“In fact, the very elab­o­rate ceil­ings, the in­tri­cate stair­case, the orig­i­nal doors and mold­ings and floors were all care­ful­ly re­fur­bished to make this her­itage house the most elab­o­rate of the sev­en man­sions,” the Na­tion­al Trust said about the ren­o­va­tion.
“The for­mer sta­bles that had been re­fur­bished to be­come of­fices were now re­pur­posed in­to a se­cu­ri­ty ac­cess point util­is­ing the back trace as a pub­lic ac­cess from the of­fi­cial car park to the west of Kil­lar­ney. The House was re-oc­cu­pied by the Prime Min­is­ter’s of­fice in Au­gust 2019.”
But de­spite these ex­ten­sive, cost­ly ren­o­va­tions, just six years lat­er in 2025 when the Unit­ed Na­tion­al Con­gress took of­fice af­ter the gen­er­al elec­tion, Pub­lic Util­i­ties Min­is­ter Bar­ry Padarath de­clared White­hall was un­fit for Prime Min­is­ter Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar to oc­cu­py.
Padarath raised sev­er­al is­sues, in­clud­ing flood­ing, mould and un­suit­abil­i­ty for mod­ern ad­min­is­tra­tive func­tions.
A year lat­er, af­ter the pre­sen­ta­tion of the 2027 Bud­get, Padarath said the build­ing re­mains ill-suit­ed for the needs of a gov­ern­ment.
The con­di­tion of White­hall was raised again af­ter $500,000 was al­lo­cat­ed in the bud­get for the con­struc­tion of a White­hall com­pan­ion build­ing.
Padarath re­vealed plans were un­der­way to find al­ter­na­tive ac­com­mo­da­tion for sev­er­al OPM de­part­ments.
He said the Cab­i­net Sec­re­tari­at was no longer housed at White­hall be­cause of long­stand­ing in­fra­struc­tur­al and op­er­a­tional chal­lenges.
In an in­ter­view with Guardian Me­dia on Oc­to­ber 29, Bisses­sar shared a sim­i­lar sen­ti­ment.

To­ba­go Car­ni­val 2026 kicked off with an in­ci­dent which of­fi­cials say did not dis­rupt the fourth year of the Oc­to­ber fes­tiv­i­ties.
A man hired to help en­sure the smooth flow of traf­fic for To­ba­go Car­ni­val was struck by a po­lice car along Wil­son Road in Scar­bor­ough yes­ter­day morn­ing. A video of the in­ci­dent, which was post­ed on­line, showed the left side of the ve­hi­cle col­lid­ing with the 40-year-old Bon Ac­cord man as it was trav­el­ling north along the street.
A me­dia re­lease from the To­ba­go Fes­ti­vals Com­mis­sion Ltd (TF­CL) said the man was a tem­po­rary work­er and did not sus­tain se­ri­ous in­juries. The com­mis­sion said the man was tak­en to the Scar­bor­ough Gen­er­al Hos­pi­tal and is in good spir­its.
The in­ci­dent came af­ter Po­lice Com­mis­sion­er Al­lis­ter Gue­var­ro, dur­ing a walk­a­bout through the J’Ou­vert cel­e­bra­tions, com­mend­ed his of­fi­cers for a safe car­ni­val.
“Ex­cel­lent job by the gold com­man­der, ex­cel­lent job by all the par­tic­i­pat­ing agen­cies, the To­ba­go Di­vi­sion, the of­fi­cers that came in to as­sist, I’m very pleased,” he said.
On the se­cu­ri­ty ap­pa­ra­tus for ma­jor events, Gue­var­ro said the TTPS has had am­ple prac­tice in the past and was well aware of what is re­quired.
“The T&T Po­lice Ser­vice has a had a num­ber of years ex­pe­ri­enc­ing with all Car­ni­val-re­lat­ed and mas events. Thus far, we have kept 100 per cent con­trol on the se­cu­ri­ty lay­out and lo­gis­tics that will be rolled out.”
He al­so thanked the pub­lic for com­ply­ing with po­lice’s re­quest on Fri­day to avoid con­fronta­tions dur­ing the fes­ti­val. He not­ed the event con­tin­ues to get bet­ter.
“As usu­al, ex­cel­lent, and con­tin­ues to grow every year. I am im­pressed.”
Gue­var­ro’s of­fi­cers kept a close eye on the ac­tiv­i­ties as thou­sands of rev­ellers flood­ed the streets of Scar­bor­ough. The late start to the J’Ou­vert did lit­tle to damp­en the ex­plo­sion of en­er­gy of the bands as mas­quer­aders made their way past the var­i­ous judg­ing points.
Min­utes be­fore po­lice shut down the J’Ou­vert around 10.23 am, one mas­quer­ad­er with a broad smile on her face shout­ed out, “To­ba­go Car­ni­val is the best and safest ever.”
The ju­bi­la­tion was ev­i­dent among rev­ellers very ear­ly as Sin City, one of the first bands to cross the stage, showed Fi­fa World Cup fever was still alive with gi­ant beach balls in­clud­ed in their pre­sen­ta­tion.
Fe­male band mem­bers wore tall socks and showed their foot­ball skills could match their win­ing abil­i­ty along Ca­lyp­so Rose Boule­vard.
Mean­while, Icon­ic band kept the tra­di­tion­al J’Ou­vert spir­it alive with a sec­tion ded­i­cat­ed to jab jab. Their bod­ies coat­ed with oil, rev­ellers en­joyed them­selves when­ev­er DJs played new So­ca Ti­tans champ Tam Tam’s win­ning song. His track, Fol­low Me, pays homage to his Grena­di­an roots. A few Grena­di­an flags were spot­ted in Icon­ic band, with some mas­quer­aders adding horns to com­plete the look.
Bago Limers brought its unique vibe to the fes­tiv­i­ties with a wa­ter truck cool­ing down rev­ellers from the in­tense heat.
Bago Limers mar­ket­ing man­ag­er Av­ery Seaton said that while Tri­nis make up the ma­jor­i­ty of peo­ple in the Car­ni­val, the in­ter­na­tion­al in­ter­est this year was at an all-time high. He said the band boasts mem­bers from the US, Lon­don and Cana­da.
“It’s like a ba­by tak­ing its first step. It crawls and then it walks. Right now we’re walk­ing, but next year get ready for the run­ning,” he said.
Seaton cred­it­ed the Bago Limers team for putting to­geth­er the pro­duc­tion so mem­bers can en­joy the road ex­pe­ri­ence.

The an­nu­al Di­vali Na­gar re­mains an im­por­tant plat­form for pre­serv­ing In­di­an cul­ture, bring­ing gen­er­a­tions to­geth­er and al­low­ing the wider na­tion­al com­mu­ni­ty to ap­pre­ci­ate the con­tri­bu­tion of In­di­an her­itage to Trinidad and To­ba­go’s mul­ti­cul­tur­al so­ci­ety.
Na­tion­al Coun­cil of In­di­an Cul­ture (NCIC) pres­i­dent Su­ru­jdeo Man­ga­roo said the Na­gar was more than a venue for en­ter­tain­ment, food and shop­ping, de­scrib­ing it as a place where cul­ture was ex­pe­ri­enced and passed on to fu­ture gen­er­a­tions.
Ad­dress­ing the open­ing of Di­vali Na­gar 2026 on Fri­day, Man­ga­roo said the an­nu­al event con­tin­ued to play an im­por­tant role in pre­serv­ing the coun­try’s cul­tur­al her­itage.
Man­ga­roo al­so thanked the hun­dreds of vol­un­teers, mer­chants, artistes, spon­sors and in­sti­tu­tions who con­tributed to stag­ing the event, de­scrib­ing their ef­forts as an ex­am­ple of what vol­un­tary ser­vice and co­op­er­a­tion could ac­com­plish.
His re­peat­ed ex­pres­sions of grat­i­tude to his board of di­rec­tors for their “sup­port and loy­al­ty” came against the back­drop of con­tro­ver­sy sur­round­ing the NCIC’s fund­ing arrange­ments for this year’s Na­gar.
The or­gan­i­sa­tion has faced scruti­ny over state agency con­tri­bu­tions.
De­spite the ten­sions, Man­ga­roo main­tained that the Na­gar’s suc­cess de­pend­ed on the col­lec­tive ef­forts of those com­mit­ted to pre­serv­ing the coun­try’s cul­tur­al her­itage.
In his ad­dress, he al­so called on the pub­lic to ex­er­cise wis­dom and dis­cern­ment in the use of ar­ti­fi­cial in­tel­li­gence, warn­ing that tech­no­log­i­cal ad­vance­ment must not come at the ex­pense of hu­man val­ues and judge­ment.
This year’s theme, Vive­ka: Dis­cern­ing Truth in an Age of AI, high­light­ed the im­por­tance of dis­tin­guish­ing be­tween truth and false­hood, right and wrong, and ben­e­fi­cial and harm­ful ac­tions in an in­creas­ing­ly tech­nol­o­gy-dri­ven world.
“Be­cause in­for­ma­tion is avail­able, does that mean it is true? And be­cause tech­nol­o­gy makes some­thing pos­si­ble, does that nec­es­sar­i­ly make it right?” he asked.
Man­ga­roo said ar­ti­fi­cial in­tel­li­gence was trans­form­ing the way peo­ple worked, learned, com­mu­ni­cat­ed and con­duct­ed busi­ness, with in­for­ma­tion that once re­quired hours of re­search now avail­able with­in sec­onds.
How­ev­er, he cau­tioned that the abil­i­ty of ma­chines to per­form in­creas­ing­ly com­plex tasks did not mean hu­mans should sur­ren­der their judge­ment to tech­nol­o­gy.
He ex­plained that Vive­ka, in Hin­du phi­los­o­phy, rep­re­sent­ed the abil­i­ty to dis­cern and recog­nise what tru­ly mat­tered.
“It is not sim­ply the abil­i­ty to know more. It is the wis­dom to know what mat­ters,” he said.
Man­ga­roo stressed that the NCIC’s theme was not an ar­gu­ment against ar­ti­fi­cial in­tel­li­gence, not­ing that the tech­nol­o­gy could as­sist doc­tors, farm­ers, busi­ness­es and stu­dents while cre­at­ing op­por­tu­ni­ties for peo­ple.
He said the chal­lenge was to em­brace tech­no­log­i­cal ad­vance­ment with­out aban­don­ing hu­man val­ues, re­spon­si­bil­i­ty and com­pas­sion.
Draw­ing a par­al­lel with the sig­nif­i­cance of Di­vali, Man­ga­roo said the fes­ti­val of lights rep­re­sent­ed more than phys­i­cal il­lu­mi­na­tion, sym­bol­is­ing knowl­edge, good­ness and the tri­umph of right­eous­ness over ig­no­rance.
“We can have the bright­est screens and still make the dark­est de­ci­sions. We can pos­sess ex­tra­or­di­nary tech­nol­o­gy and still lack com­pas­sion,” he said.
He added that knowl­edge must be guid­ed by dhar­ma, pow­er by re­spon­si­bil­i­ty and progress mea­sured not on­ly by tech­no­log­i­cal achieve­ments but al­so by the qual­i­ty of hu­man be­ings so­ci­ety pro­duced.
There was a heavy pres­ence of po­lice and se­cu­ri­ty at the Na­gar. Se­nior Su­per­in­ten­dent Rudolph Bhag­wan­deen told GML that there were at least 40 po­lice­men in­side and out­side the venue.

Chris­t­ian Church­es are study­ing a new law passed by Par­lia­ment that could make the tra­di­tion­al sip of wine tak­en by chil­dren and teenagers dur­ing Holy Com­mu­nion a $50,000 of­fence, and plans to make rep­re­sen­ta­tions be­fore Christ­mas.
An­gli­can Bish­op Right Rev­erend Claude Berkley said the law di­rect­ly af­fects the rite, which has been prac­tised by gen­er­a­tions of Chris­tians.
“This is an en­shrined rit­u­al of the Church from very ear­ly times.”
Holy Com­mu­nion, al­so called the Eu­charist, is a cen­tral rite in many Chris­t­ian church­es. It traces to the Last Sup­per in the Gospels, where Je­sus shared bread and wine with his dis­ci­ples. In Catholic teach­ing, the bread and wine be­come the body and blood of Christ, while oth­er de­nom­i­na­tions hold dif­fer­ent views.
Berkley said the Church was study­ing the law and, if it re­mained in force, “the Church is com­pelled to obey the law of the land.”
The Mis­cel­la­neous Pro­vi­sions (Al­co­hol, Cannabis, Dan­ger­ous Drugs, Gam­bling and To­bac­co) Bill, 2026, rais­es the le­gal age for al­co­hol and to­bac­co from 18 to 21, and for cannabis and gam­bling to 25. It makes it an of­fence for any­one aged 18 to 20, or a child over ten, to drink or pos­sess al­co­hol, and for any­one to know­ing­ly sell it to some­one un­der 21. The penal­ty is a $50,000 fine, though po­lice may is­sue a fixed penal­ty no­tice that can be paid or set­tled through a re­ha­bil­i­ta­tive pro­gramme.
As in­tro­duced, the Bill has no ex­emp­tion for re­li­gious or sacra­men­tal al­co­hol. Berkley said the Church’s think­ing is that an ex­press ex­emp­tion is need­ed, but it has not con­clud­ed on that.
An­gli­cans use a low-al­co­hol wine, Berkley said. The Church once im­port­ed an of­fi­cial com­mu­nion wine that is no longer avail­able and now of­ten buys from the Ro­man Catholic Church. Chil­dren and teenagers have tak­en it, he said, and the Church has not had an is­sue.
In the House last week, Op­po­si­tion MP Colm Im­bert linked the cannabis amend­ments to lim­its on sacra­men­tal wine at com­mu­nion. At­tor­ney Gen­er­al John Je­re­mie re­ject­ed his in­ter­pre­ta­tion and called his claims “in­flam­ma­to­ry and de­void of mer­it.”
Im­bert re­peat­ed the charge on X on Fri­day, post­ing that the UNC Gov­ern­ment had just passed a law which “im­pos­es an out­right ban on the dis­pens­ing of sacra­men­tal wine to Catholics and oth­er Chris­tians un­der the age of 21 dur­ing com­mu­nion, with harsh penal­ties.” He al­so claimed no oth­er Com­mon­wealth coun­try has such a law.
Not every church is af­fect­ed. Spir­i­tu­al Bap­tist leader King Shep­erd Ray Brath­waite said his faith us­es non-al­co­holic wine through­out the coun­try.
Berkley said he does not re­call any con­sul­ta­tion with the An­gli­can Church. IRO pres­i­dent Dr El­lis Bur­ris said it did not con­sult the Gov­ern­ment or the At­tor­ney Gen­er­al.
“We will not ask any ques­tions.”
The IRO will ta­ble the Bill at its meet­ing on No­vem­ber 21.
The Catholic Arch­dio­cese is aware of the is­sue. Guardian Me­dia reached out for com­ment and is await­ing a re­sponse.
Par­lia­ment com­plet­ed its pas­sage of the Bill last week when the House ap­proved two amend­ments from the Sen­ate.

A search for a kid­napped Venezue­lan teenag­er has re­sult­ed in the dis­cov­ery of a sus­pect­ed hu­man traf­fick­ing ring.
Ac­cord­ing to a press re­lease from the T&T Po­lice Ser­vice (TTPS), of­fi­cers of the West­ern Di­vi­sion led by Deputy Po­lice Com­mis­sion­er (DCP) Suzette Mar­tin made the dis­cov­ery while search­ing an apart­ment build­ing in Cunu­pia for a Venezue­lan teenag­er, who was al­leged­ly kid­napped and brought to Trinidad.
The of­fi­cers found 16 Venezue­lan na­tion­als in one apart­ment, in­clud­ing the re­port­ed vic­tim and an­oth­er mi­nor.
Two of the Venezue­lan women, ages 20 and 19, were ar­rest­ed as they were iden­ti­fied as the sus­pects in the kid­nap­ping.
A 55-year-old Trinida­di­an man from Cunu­pia was al­so held.
The mi­nors and the oth­er women re­mained in po­lice cus­tody at dif­fer­ent sta­tions in west Trinidad, up to late yes­ter­day.
Act­ing Sgt Hug­gins is con­tin­u­ing in­ves­ti­ga­tions in­to the in­ci­dent. —Derek Achong
Dozens ar­rest­ed dur­ing po­lice ex­er­cis­es in north, south, and east Trinidad
Sev­er­al dozen per­sons were ar­rest­ed by the po­lice in si­mul­ta­ne­ous ex­er­cis­es in north, east and south Trinidad be­tween Fri­day night and yes­ter­day morn­ing.
Ac­cord­ing to press re­leas­es is­sued by the T&T Po­lice Ser­vice (TTPS) yes­ter­day af­ter­noon, one ex­er­cise in north­ern Trinidad re­sult­ed in 12 peo­ple be­ing ar­rest­ed and 11 war­rants be­ing ex­e­cut­ed in Mal­abar and Cu­mu­to.
The war­rants re­lat­ed to out­stand­ing court-or­dered pay­ments against eight men, to­talling $57,733.57.
Four of the de­tainees were held in Ari­ma for lar­ce­ny-re­lat­ed and out­stand­ing war­rant en­quiries by of­fi­cers, who were fo­cus­ing on stolen ve­hi­cles.
A sep­a­rate ex­er­cise in Arou­ca re­sult­ed in four ar­rests, in­clud­ing one man who was want­ed for as­sault by beat­ing and an­oth­er want­ed for fail­ing to pay an $800 fine.
Thir­ty-two peo­ple were ar­rest­ed in a sep­a­rate ex­er­cise in south Trinidad. Thir­teen of those ar­rest­ed were held on out­stand­ing com­mit­ment war­rants for sums rang­ing from $1,500 to $65,000.
In Princes Town and Bar­rack­pore, two men were held for pos­ses­sion of knives, one for mar­i­jua­na pos­ses­sion, one for co­caine pos­ses­sion, and one for wear­ing cam­ou­flage cloth­ing.
The of­fi­cers al­so is­sued nu­mer­ous fixed penal­ty tick­ets for dri­ving of­fences.
Mean­while, an ex­er­cise in east­ern Trinidad re­sult­ed in 23 ar­rests.
Eigh­teen were ar­rest­ed in San­gre Grande for out­stand­ing war­rants. One man from San Souci was ar­rest­ed near Ba­lan­dra for be­ing in pos­ses­sion of  126 grammes of mar­i­jua­na.
Po­lice of­fi­cers in Rio Claro al­so raid­ed a bar, searched the pa­trons and ar­rest­ed three of them.
One man was ar­rest­ed as part of a rob­bery in­ves­ti­ga­tion, while the oth­er was held for a wound­ing probe. The third man was ar­rest­ed for us­ing ob­scene lan­guage and re­sist­ing ar­rest.

To­ba­go Car­ni­val’s J’ou­vert cel­e­bra­tions end­ed with­out any ar­rests or se­ri­ous in­ci­dents on Sat­ur­day morn­ing, with po­lice re­port­ing a large­ly in­ci­dent-free start to the fes­tiv­i­ties.
The cel­e­bra­tions ran from 4 am to 10 am, as rev­ellers took to the streets with paint, mud and oil.
In a state­ment, the Trinidad and To­ba­go Po­lice Ser­vice (TTPS) said of­fi­cers main­tained a high­ly vis­i­ble pres­ence through­out the com­pe­ti­tion and pa­rade ar­eas.
How­ev­er, one in­ci­dent was record­ed along Wil­son Road, Scar­bor­ough, where a marked po­lice ve­hi­cle al­leged­ly col­lid­ed with a 40-year-old To­ba­go Fes­ti­vals Com­mis­sion em­ploy­ee from Bon Ac­cord.
The in­ci­dent oc­curred as the ve­hi­cle was trav­el­ling north along Wil­son Road.
The man was tak­en for med­ical at­ten­tion and is re­port­ed to have sus­tained mi­nor in­juries. The ac­ci­dent is un­der in­ves­ti­ga­tion.
Com­mis­sion­er of Po­lice Al­lis­ter Gue­var­ro and Deputy Com­mis­sion­er of Po­lice (Op­er­a­tions) Suzette Mar­tin were among se­nior of­fi­cers on the ground through­out the morn­ing.
Gue­var­ro was al­so seen walk­ing along the pa­rade routes, in­ter­act­ing with of­fi­cers and rev­ellers.
The po­lice en­tourage in­clud­ed As­sis­tant Com­mis­sion­er Anand Rame­sar, Se­nior Su­per­in­ten­dents Clint Arthur and Ro­hdill Kirk, Su­per­in­ten­dent Mark Joseph and of­fi­cers of the To­ba­go Di­vi­sion.
The Com­mis­sion­er al­so vis­it­ed the Shir­van Road Po­lice Sta­tion and the Ply­mouth Mi­cro Po­lice Unit, where he in­ter­act­ed with of­fi­cers on du­ty.
The polic­ing op­er­a­tion in­volved of­fi­cers from the In­ter-Agency Task Force, Guard and Emer­gency Branch and To­ba­go Di­vi­sion.
They were sup­port­ed by sea pa­trols from the Coastal Sup­port Unit, un­der the com­mand of Act­ing As­sis­tant Su­per­in­ten­dent Ron­nie Ram­pal­ad, as well as air sup­port.
The TTPS said of­fi­cers would main­tain their pres­ence through­out the re­main­der of the Car­ni­val cel­e­bra­tions, in­clud­ing the Pa­rade of the Bands and oth­er sched­uled events.
The Ser­vice thanked rev­ellers, vis­i­tors and mem­bers of the pub­lic for com­ply­ing with the law and urged them to con­tin­ue ex­er­cis­ing safe­ty pre­cau­tions.

Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar and United States Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau shake hands during the visit by the Deputy Secretary and his delegation for high-level bilateral engagements at the Diplomatic Centre, St Ann's yesterday.
COURTESY:US EMBASSY
US Deputy Sec­re­tary of State Christo­pher Lan­dau has thanked Prime Min­is­ter Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar and the Gov­ern­ment of Trinidad and To­ba­go for sup­port­ing calls for de­mo­c­ra­t­ic change in Cu­ba.
In a post on X on Fri­day, Lan­dau said the Unit­ed States recog­nised and ap­pre­ci­at­ed Trinidad and To­ba­go’s vote in favour of what he de­scribed as a de­mo­c­ra­t­ic tran­si­tion in Cu­ba at the Unit­ed Na­tions this year.
“We’re proud to stand along­side Trinidad & To­ba­go and oth­er democ­ra­cies in the re­gion in call­ing out the re­pres­sive Cuban regime,” he said.
Lan­dau ques­tioned how coun­tries could sup­port a gov­ern­ment which, he claimed, had not al­lowed its peo­ple to vote for al­most 68 years.
“How can coun­tries vote in fa­vor of a regime that has not al­lowed its own peo­ple to vote for al­most 68 YEARS?!” he wrote.
He al­so ex­tend­ed his best wish­es to Per­sad-Bisses­sar and the peo­ple of Trinidad and To­ba­go, re­call­ing that he was proud to have vis­it­ed the coun­try a few months ago.
Per­sad-Bisses­sar re­spond­ed by thank­ing Lan­dau for his com­ments and reaf­firm­ing the Gov­ern­ment’s po­si­tion on democ­ra­cy, free­dom and hu­man rights.
“The Gov­ern­ment of Trinidad and To­ba­go stands for democ­ra­cy, free­dom, hu­man dig­ni­ty and the right of every cit­i­zen, in­clud­ing the peo­ple of Cu­ba, to freely de­ter­mine their po­lit­i­cal fu­ture,” she said.
The ex­change fol­lows Trinidad and To­ba­go’s con­tro­ver­sial vote at the Unit­ed Na­tions Gen­er­al As­sem­bly on Wednes­day, when the coun­try joined the Unit­ed States in op­pos­ing a res­o­lu­tion call­ing for an end to the US eco­nom­ic, com­mer­cial and fi­nan­cial em­bar­go on Cu­ba.
It marked a sig­nif­i­cant de­par­ture from T&T’s long­stand­ing po­si­tion on the is­sue. The coun­try had vot­ed in favour of lift­ing the em­bar­go every year since 1993, hav­ing ab­stained when the res­o­lu­tion was first in­tro­duced in 1992.
De­spite T&T’s op­po­si­tion, the res­o­lu­tion was adopt­ed, with 130 coun­tries vot­ing in favour, 17 against and 25 ab­stain­ing.
The res­o­lu­tion, which is non-bind­ing, was the 34th an­nu­al call by the Gen­er­al As­sem­bly for an end to the US em­bar­go.
The Gov­ern­ment has de­fend­ed its vote on the grounds that it sup­ports democ­ra­cy and po­lit­i­cal free­doms for the Cuban peo­ple.

Two sus­pects have been ar­rest­ed and 16 Venezue­lan na­tion­als, in­clud­ing two mi­nors, were found dur­ing an in­tel­li­gence-led an­ti-crime ex­er­cise in Cunu­pia amid in­ves­ti­ga­tions in­to a re­port­ed kid­nap­ping.
The ex­er­cise was con­duct­ed by of­fi­cers of the West­ern Di­vi­sion un­der Op­er­a­tion R.E.S.O.L.U.T.E. Shield be­tween 7pm on Fri­day, Oc­to­ber 30, and 12.15am on Sat­ur­day, Oc­to­ber 31.
Ac­cord­ing to a po­lice state­ment, of­fi­cers act­ed on in­for­ma­tion about a pos­si­ble kid­nap­ping orig­i­nat­ing from Venezuela and re­ports that mi­nors were al­leged­ly be­ing kept at a par­tic­u­lar lo­ca­tion.
Of­fi­cers pro­ceed­ed to a two-storey, 14-apart­ment build­ing along Ramdeen Dri­ve, En­deav­our Link Up Road, Cunu­pia, where they searched Apart­ment No. 7.
Dur­ing the search, they found 16 Venezue­lan na­tion­als, in­clud­ing the re­port­ed vic­tim and an­oth­er mi­nor.
Two Venezue­lan women, aged 20 and 19, who were iden­ti­fied as sus­pects in the kid­nap­ping re­port, were ar­rest­ed and tak­en to the Four Roads Po­lice Sta­tion.
A 55-year-old Cunu­pia man was al­so ar­rest­ed and tak­en to the West End Po­lice Sta­tion.
The two mi­nors were tak­en to the West End Po­lice Sta­tion, while 12 oth­er Venezue­lan women were tak­en to the Care­nage Po­lice Sta­tion.
Of­fi­cers of the Cen­tral Crime Scene Unit sub­se­quent­ly pho­tographed and processed the scene, seiz­ing sev­er­al cel­lu­lar phones, doc­u­ments, a dig­i­tal video recorder (DVR) and oth­er items con­sid­ered to be of ev­i­den­tial val­ue.
The ex­er­cise was spear­head­ed by Deputy Com­mis­sion­er of Po­lice Suzette Mar­tin, As­sis­tant Com­mis­sion­er of Po­lice Hen­ry and Se­nior Su­per­in­ten­dent Williams.
In­ves­ti­ga­tions are con­tin­u­ing un­der the su­per­vi­sion of Act­ing Sergeant Hug­gins.
