A trade union leader yes­ter­day called on Gov­ern­ment to keep the promis­es it made dur­ing the cam­paign trail and al­so chal­lenged oth­er union lead­ers, whom he said had lost their way, to stand with work­ers or step aside, warn­ing that sol­i­dar­i­ty could not be prac­tised on­ly when con­ve­nient.
Speak­ing at the labour move­ment’s ral­ly in Wood­ford Square fol­low­ing a march through Port-of-Spain, Steel Work­ers’ Union of T&T pres­i­dent Tim­o­thy Bai­ley urged trade union­ists to put work­ers’ in­ter­ests ahead of per­son­al con­sid­er­a­tions.
“I do not want to be­lieve you are sell­outs. So, I call on my com­rades who have lost their way to un­der­stand that sol­i­dar­i­ty is for­ev­er. It is not a con­ve­nient thing. It is for­ev­er. Do right by the work­ing class. Do your job or leave the job,” he said.
Bai­ley said pub­lic fig­ures, ac­tivists, trade union­ists and oth­ers in po­si­tions of au­thor­i­ty should not be afraid to speak out on is­sues, even when do­ing so could car­ry per­son­al con­se­quences.
He named no union in his ap­peal, which came amid di­vi­sions over par­tic­i­pa­tion in the demon­stra­tion. Oil­fields Work­ers’ Trade Union pres­i­dent gen­er­al An­cel Ro­get had pre­vi­ous­ly said his union would not of­fi­cial­ly par­tic­i­pate be­cause mem­bers were prepar­ing for ne­go­ti­a­tions. The Pub­lic Ser­vices As­so­ci­a­tion, led by Fe­l­isha Thomas, al­so did not par­tic­i­pate in the march.
Bai­ley al­so ac­cused Prime Min­is­ter Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar of fail­ing to ho­n­our cam­paign promis­es, re­ject­ing sug­ges­tions that work­ers should re­main silent while wait­ing for the Unit­ed Na­tion­al Con­gress-led Gov­ern­ment to act.
“Ho­n­ourable Prime Min­is­ter, on your cam­paign trail you promised the peo­ple of Trinidad and To­ba­go a lot of things and you have not de­liv­ered on your promis­es,” he said.
“Do you want to muz­zle the peo­ple? We are say­ing that can­not hap­pen.”
He al­so re­ject­ed claims that unions had re­mained silent dur­ing the pre­vi­ous Peo­ple’s Na­tion­al Move­ment (PNM) ad­min­is­tra­tion and were now tar­get­ing the UNC Gov­ern­ment.
Hold­ing up a news­pa­per re­port of an ear­li­er protest against for­mer prime min­is­ter Dr Kei­th Row­ley, Bai­ley point­ed to his union’s ac­tivism since the clo­sure of the steel in­dus­try in 2016.
“The trade union move­ment has nev­er been silent and the trade union move­ment will nev­er be silent,” he said.
Bai­ley ar­gued that the in­dus­try’s clo­sure had cost the coun­try jobs, eco­nom­ic ac­tiv­i­ty and for­eign ex­change earn­ings, while leav­ing dis­placed work­ers strug­gling for com­pen­sa­tion.
“You can­not re­open a steel in­dus­try and side­line the steel work­ers who built the in­dus­try,” he said.
He added, “Will we con­tin­ue with a re­volv­ing door of pol­i­tics where you promise peo­ple and do not de­liv­er?”
He al­so called for pro­posed amend­ments to the Re­trench­ment and Sev­er­ance Ben­e­fits Act to be brought be­fore Par­lia­ment ur­gent­ly, ar­gu­ing that em­ploy­ees re­mained vul­ner­a­ble when com­pa­nies shut down with­out pay­ing work­ers their en­ti­tle­ments.
Ahead of the march, Per­sad-Bisses­sar de­fend­ed her ad­min­is­tra­tion’s record, say­ing it was set­tling back­pay, up­dat­ing salaries, of­fer­ing 10 per cent wage in­creas­es and ad­vanc­ing leg­is­la­tion aimed at pro­tect­ing work­ers.
She al­so ac­cused the protest of be­ing dri­ven by po­lit­i­cal and racial hos­til­i­ty, ques­tion­ing unions’ de­ci­sion to march along­side rep­re­sen­ta­tives of the for­mer ad­min­is­tra­tion.
Bai­ley, how­ev­er, told sup­port­ers the demon­stra­tion marked on­ly the be­gin­ning and urged work­ers to recog­nise their role in shap­ing the coun­try’s fu­ture.
Com­mu­ni­ca­tion Work­ers’ Union sec­re­tary gen­er­al Joanne Ogeer al­so crit­i­cised the ad­min­is­tra­tion’s treat­ment of dis­sent, warn­ing that po­lit­i­cal pow­er did not give lead­ers the right to hu­mil­i­ate cit­i­zens.
De­scrib­ing the demon­stra­tion as a per­for­mance ap­praisal of the Gov­ern­ment, she re­mind­ed lead­ers that vot­ers would ul­ti­mate­ly de­cide whether to re­new their man­date.
“You are not the own­ers of this coun­try. You are the tem­po­rary cus­to­di­ans of the peo­ple’s trust,” Ogeer said.
She ac­cused the ad­min­is­tra­tion of aban­don­ing the hu­mil­i­ty it dis­played be­fore tak­ing of­fice and ar­gued that work­ers’ hard­ships could not be dis­missed through par­ti­san la­bels.
“A hun­gry child does not ask whether their par­ents vot­ed UNC or PNM. A re­trenched work­er does not pay their mort­gage with a par­ty card,” she said.
Ogeer urged cit­i­zens to de­fend peace­ful protest, re­ject racial di­vi­sion and de­mand ac­count­abil­i­ty be­tween elec­tions.
“You can­not preach democ­ra­cy dur­ing an elec­tion cam­paign and prac­tise in­tol­er­ance af­ter win­ning,” she said.
Es­tate Po­lice As­so­ci­a­tion pres­i­dent Deryck Richard­son mean­while di­rect­ed crit­i­cism at suc­ces­sive ad­min­is­tra­tions, ac­cus­ing them of fail­ing se­cu­ri­ty of­fi­cers and re­tirees.
Ac­knowl­edg­ing PNM rep­re­sen­ta­tives at the march, he chal­lenged their record while in gov­ern­ment.
“Where were you when we need­ed you? We plead­ed, we cried, we marched, and noth­ing,” he said.
Richard­son called for a spe­cial in­dus­tri­al frame­work for se­cu­ri­ty work­ers, a liv­ing wage, over­time af­ter eight hours, an­nu­al and sick leave, paid uni­forms, prop­er train­ing and time­ly pay­ment of wages.
He al­so de­mand­ed set­tle­ment of out­stand­ing re­tire­ment ben­e­fits and wage ne­go­ti­a­tions, in­sist­ing that mon­ey owed to work­ers was a debt, not a po­lit­i­cal favour.
“They come for your vote. They make promis­es. And af­ter elec­tions, too many work­ers are ex­pect­ed to be qui­et while their rights are de­nied,” Richard­son said.
Sea­men and Wa­ter­front Work­ers’ Trade Union pres­i­dent Michael An­nisette, who al­so serves as NATUC’s gen­er­al sec­re­tary, de­mand­ed the set­tle­ment of all out­stand­ing col­lec­tive agree­ments. He said it was un­ac­cept­able that work­ers re­mained on salaries dat­ing back to 2012 and 2013 while fac­ing the re­al­i­ties of the cost of liv­ing in 2026.
An­nisette al­so re­ject­ed the Prime Min­is­ter’s sug­ges­tion that unions protest­ed on­ly when an In­di­an prime min­is­ter held of­fice, cit­ing demon­stra­tions un­der the pre­vi­ous PNM ad­min­is­tra­tion over Petrotrin’s clo­sure, wage of­fers and salary in­creas­es for se­nior pub­lic of­fi­cials.
“We chal­lenged the PNM when it was in of­fice. We will hold the UNC ac­count­able while it is in of­fice and we make no apolo­gies for that,” he said.
“That is not be­tray­al, it is trade union­ism.”
An­nisette main­tained that or­gan­ised labour’s re­spon­si­bil­i­ty was to work­ers, pen­sion­ers and their fam­i­lies, re­gard­less of which par­ty was in pow­er.
“The labour move­ment did not dis­cov­er in­jus­tice af­ter the PNM left of­fice. We have chal­lenged it con­sis­tent­ly,” he said.
The NATUC-or­gan­ised protest be­gan short­ly af­ter 9 am at Memo­r­i­al Park, draw­ing hun­dreds of union mem­bers, op­po­si­tion par­ty mem­bers and oth­er par­tic­i­pants.
Op­po­si­tion Leader Pen­ne­lope Beck­les, MP Stu­art Young and Pa­tri­ot­ic Front leader Mick­ela Pan­day were among those in at­ten­dance.
Work­ers marched over un­re­solved wage ne­go­ti­a­tions, out­stand­ing pay­ments, re­trench­ment and broad­er con­cerns about the UNC’s gov­er­nance of coun­try.
The protest had been post­poned from Oc­to­ber 16 to ac­com­mo­date the state-as­sist­ed fu­ner­al of ca­lyp­son­ian Slinger “Mighty Spar­row” Fran­cis­co.
Or­gan­is­ers lat­er re­ject­ed an­oth­er re­quest for post­pone­ment, which An­nisette said po­lice at­trib­uted to re­sources be­ing com­mit­ted to To­ba­go Car­ni­val.

jensen.lavende@guardian.co.tt
Armed with plac­ards, pam­phlets, flags, ban­ners, blowhorns, snow cones and their voic­es, trade union mem­bers marched from Memo­r­i­al Park to Wood­ford Square in Port-of-Spain yes­ter­day, in a bid to pres­sure the Gov­ern­ment to con­clude long-stand­ing wage ne­go­ti­a­tions.
At the start of the march, Na­tion­al Trade Union Cen­tre (NATUC) gen­er­al sec­re­tary Michael An­nisette de­scribed the event as a “spir­i­tu­al.”
How­ev­er, as the pro­ces­sion moved along St Clair Av­enue and passed the Of­fice of the Prime Min­is­ter, the at­mos­phere ap­peared to take on a more an­ti-gov­ern­ment tone.
Some par­tic­i­pants waved flags, sound­ed horns and chant­ed, “Kam­la must go,” while em­ploy­ees at the Of­fice of the Prime Min­is­ter looked on and record­ed the demon­stra­tion.
Po­lice of­fi­cers re­peat­ed­ly urged marchers to keep mov­ing as danc­ing and cel­e­bra­tions in­ten­si­fied out­side the build­ing.
Se­cu­ri­ty was high­ly vis­i­ble through­out the route, with at least five po­lice ve­hi­cles, in­clud­ing a 26-seater truck car­ry­ing of­fi­cers in ri­ot gear, ac­com­pa­ny­ing the pro­ces­sion. Oth­er of­fi­cers marched among par­tic­i­pants or trav­elled along­side the mu­sic truck and at the front of the crowd.
Se­nior po­lice of­fi­cers were un­able to pro­vide an es­ti­mate of the crowd size up to press time.
Among the unions rep­re­sent­ed were the Com­mu­ni­ca­tion Work­ers’ Union (CWU), Trinidad and To­ba­go Reg­is­tered Nurs­es As­so­ci­a­tion (TTR­NA), Trinidad and To­ba­go Uni­fied Teach­ers’ As­so­ci­a­tion (TTUTA), Sea­men and Wa­ter­front Work­ers’ Trade Union (SWW­TU), Con­trac­tors and Gen­er­al Work­ers’ Trade Union (CG­WU) and the Steel Work­ers Union of Trinidad and To­ba­go (SWUTT).
No­tably ab­sent were the Pub­lic Ser­vices As­so­ci­a­tion (PSA) and the Oil­fields Work­ers’ Trade Union (OW­TU), both mem­bers of the Gov­ern­ment’s Coali­tion of In­ter­ests.
De­spite sharp crit­i­cism from the Gov­ern­ment be­fore and through­out the demon­stra­tion, union and po­lit­i­cal lead­ers al­so re­peat­ed­ly in­sist­ed the march was not po­lit­i­cal­ly mo­ti­vat­ed.
On Thurs­day, Prime Min­is­ter Kam­la Per­sad-Bisses­sar urged cit­i­zens, par­tic­u­lar­ly her sup­port­ers, to avoid the cap­i­tal dur­ing the protest, al­leg­ing that the 12 par­tic­i­pat­ing trade unions har­boured po­lit­i­cal and racial hos­til­i­ty to­wards her ad­min­is­tra­tion.
How­ev­er, Op­po­si­tion Leader Pen­ne­lope Beck­les re­ject­ed that claim yes­ter­day, say­ing the at­ten­dance of po­lit­i­cal fig­ures was not an at­tempt to score po­lit­i­cal points.
“The Prime Min­is­ter prob­a­bly has a short mem­o­ry that she has marched many times with trade unions. This here is about sol­i­dar­i­ty with the trade union move­ment. We know that there are is­sues. The Prime Min­is­ter may have set­tled some of her is­sues with some unions, but there are still unions where wages, salaries and is­sues re­lat­ing to the cost of liv­ing still arise. So I am not re­al­ly con­cerned about how she feels about it,” Beck­les said.
For­mer prime min­is­ter Stu­art Young echoed those sen­ti­ments, say­ing he at­tend­ed as a cit­i­zen sup­port­ing work­ers frus­trat­ed by pro­tract­ed wage ne­go­ti­a­tions.
Pa­tri­ot­ic Front leader Mick­ela Pan­day al­so dis­missed the Prime Min­is­ter’s com­ments, ac­cus­ing her of try­ing to politi­cise the demon­stra­tion.
“I don’t ex­pect the Prime Min­is­ter to say any­thing else. What else can she say? Do you ex­pect her to say this is a ral­ly of the peo­ple’s dis­en­chant­ment with how my Gov­ern­ment has been per­form­ing for over a year and a half? She’s not go­ing to say that. What I take um­brage with is bring­ing race in­to it,” Pan­day said.
The march, sched­uled to be­gin at 9 am, start­ed near­ly two hours late and took about two hours to reach Wood­ford Square, where union lead­ers ad­dressed sup­port­ers and com­plained about the slow pace of wage ne­go­ti­a­tions.
Along the route, par­tic­i­pants kept cool with wa­ter, snow cones, lol­lies and the oc­ca­sion­al beer.
Po­lit­i­cal lead­ers al­so stopped near Queen’s Roy­al Col­lege, en­cour­ag­ing stu­dents ob­serv­ing the march to fo­cus on their ed­u­ca­tion be­fore en­ter­ing pol­i­tics.
At Wood­ford Square, union rep­re­sen­ta­tives re­newed calls for the Gov­ern­ment to ac­cel­er­ate wage talks and ad­dress work­ers’ con­cerns over salaries and the ris­ing cost of liv­ing.
PSA boss con­demns protest
Pub­lic Ser­vices As­so­ci­a­tion pres­i­dent Fe­l­isha Thomas yes­ter­day crit­i­cised the protest march, de­scrib­ing it as a be­tray­al of the work­ers the union lead­ers claimed to be rep­re­sent­ing.
“I will not walk with the very per­sons who caused the very work­ers they are pre­tend­ing to care about to re­main on 2013 salaries, de­stroyed the lives of thou­sands in Petrotrin and TSTT, and dis­tressed thou­sands of work­ers in BIR, Cus­toms, WASA and many more,” Thomas said in a What­sApp re­sponse to ques­tions from Guardian Me­dia on her union’s de­ci­sion not to par­tic­i­pate in the protest march.
She added, “I can­not and will not pre­tend that the cur­rent state of this coun­try is not a di­rect re­sult of the poor gov­er­nance of the PNM and their lack of care for the peo­ple of this coun­try.”
De­spite the OW­TU’s ab­sence from the event as well, one shop stew­ard who re­quest­ed anonymi­ty said he at­tend­ed in his per­son­al ca­pac­i­ty.
“I am a mem­ber of the OW­TU who is dis­pleased with the state of the coun­try. I am a mem­ber of the OW­TU who is dis­pleased with the lead­er­ship of the OW­TU. I rep­re­sent the OW­TU as a mem­ber, and I am mak­ing a stand,” he said.
He added, “My leader got one kiss from the Prime Min­is­ter and ap­par­ent­ly he took it for love. I ain’t get no love. I want love. I want love for the coun­try. One kiss can’t help me.”

Se­nior Re­porter
eliz­a­beth.gon­za­les@guardian.co.tt
Po­lice record­ed more than 40,000 re­ports un­der the Lar­ce­ny Act over al­most six years. How­ev­er, few­er than 8,000 of­fences led to a sus­pect be­ing ar­rest­ed and charged.
The re­ports in­clud­ed rob­bery, theft, fraud and break-ins. Be­tween 1 Jan­u­ary 2021 and 30 Sep­tem­ber 2026, po­lice record­ed 40,846 of­fences. Of these, 7,924 were list­ed as de­tect­ed. That leaves 32,922 of­fences, or 80.6 per cent, not record­ed as de­tect­ed.
At­tor­ney Keron Ramkhal­whan ob­tained the fig­ures un­der the Free­dom of In­for­ma­tion Act for his client, Vishal Per­sad. They were pre­pared by the Trinidad and To­ba­go Po­lice Ser­vice’s Crime and Prob­lem Analy­sis Branch. The fig­ures are dat­ed 27 Oc­to­ber 2026 and are pro­vi­sion­al, mean­ing they may be re­vised.
A de­tec­tion means a sus­pect has been ar­rest­ed and charged. It does not mean the per­son has been found guilty in court.
Po­lice se­nior of­fi­cials have spo­ken be­fore about the need to im­prove de­tec­tion. At a par­lia­men­tary com­mit­tee hear­ing on 17 May 2023, then act­ing Deputy Com­mis­sion­er Curt Si­mon said “we are not com­fort­able with our de­tec­tion rate”.
Then po­lice com­mis­sion­er Er­la Hare­wood-Christo­pher said train­ing and tech­nol­o­gy were pri­or­i­ties. Po­lice were bring­ing back ex­pe­ri­enced re­tired in­ves­ti­ga­tors to train of­fi­cers, she said.
The records cov­er all ten po­lice di­vi­sions. Rob­bery was the largest cat­e­go­ry, with 12,453 re­ports. This was fol­lowed by gen­er­al theft, with 10,696, and break­ing-in of­fences, with 8,877. The re­main­ing re­ports were for ve­hi­cle theft, fraud and oth­er of­fences.
North Cen­tral had the low­est de­tec­tion rate, at 9.8 per cent. Po­lice record­ed 4,386 re­ports and 431 de­tec­tions. That means few­er than one in ten of the di­vi­sion’s re­port­ed of­fences led to an ar­rest and charge. Port-of-Spain’s rate was 11.6 per cent. North­ern Di­vi­sion’s was 11.8 per cent.
East­ern had the high­est rate, at 44.7 per cent. This was still few­er than half of its re­port­ed of­fences. Cen­tral had the most re­ports, with 6,560, and record­ed 1,320 de­tec­tions. In To­ba­go, 547 of the 2,566 re­port­ed of­fences were de­tect­ed.
The ve­hi­cle theft fig­ures showed 4,966 re­ports and 90 peo­ple record­ed as ar­rest­ed and charged. Cen­tral ac­count­ed for 53 of those per­sons, fol­lowed by South­ern with ten and North­ern with eight.
The records al­so list­ed 10,599 peo­ple as ar­rest­ed and charged un­der the Act. That fig­ure counts peo­ple. The 7,924 fig­ure counts of­fences. More than one per­son can be charged for the same of­fence. The records did not give a sep­a­rate de­tec­tion to­tal for ve­hi­cle theft.
In Au­gust 2026, Se­nior Su­per­in­ten­dent Rudolph Bhag­wan­deen de­scribed how Cen­tral Di­vi­sion was tack­ling ve­hi­cle theft. He said of­fi­cers were work­ing to share in­for­ma­tion faster, re­cov­er stolen ve­hi­cles and tar­get ar­eas where these crimes oc­curred.
The Po­lice Ser­vice Com­mis­sion’s 2024 sur­vey al­so record­ed con­cerns about po­lice fol­low-up. It re­ceived 3,887 re­spons­es be­tween Sep­tem­ber and Oc­to­ber. About 63 per­cent did not be­lieve po­lice fol­lowed up re­ports. About 65 per­cent did not be­lieve po­lice gave feed­back.
The same sur­vey found that 79 per­cent feared be­ing a vic­tim of rob­bery, house­break­ing or home in­va­sion.
Po­lice have al­so re­port­ed progress in fight­ing crime. In Sep­tem­ber 2025, Com­mis­sion­er Al­lis­ter Gue­var­ro said na­tion­al de­tec­tion rates had in­creased from 30 to 35 per­cent af­ter the state of emer­gency be­gan that Ju­ly.
In its third quar­ter 2026 pub­lic per­for­mance ap­praisal, showed that 265 homi­cides were record­ed be­tween Jan­u­ary and Sep­tem­ber this year, a 3.6 per cent de­crease com­pared with the cor­re­spond­ing pe­ri­od in 2025 and a 44.2 per cent de­cline com­pared with 2024.
It al­so showed that se­ri­ous re­port­ed crime fell to 7,593 in­ci­dents, rep­re­sent­ing a 13.3 per cent re­duc­tion com­pared with the 2025 fig­ure and a 17.3 per cent de­crease com­pared with 2024.
The FOIA al­so showed that the num­ber of re­ports fell from 8,015 in 2023 to 7,451 in 2024 and 6,890 in 2025. The 2026 to­tal of 4,377 cov­ers Jan­u­ary to Sep­tem­ber on­ly.
Rob­beries were re­port­ed far more of­ten than mur­ders in 2024. Po­lice record­ed 2,400 rob­beries, com­pared with 625 mur­ders. There were al­so 1,695 re­ports of gen­er­al theft, 1,613 break­ing of­fences and 1,090 ve­hi­cle thefts.
The FOIA records pro­vide no con­vic­tion fig­ures. They al­so do not ex­plain why 32,922 re­port­ed of­fences were not record­ed as de­tect­ed.

A 42-year-old Wood­brook busi­ness­woman has sued the State, al­leg­ing that she was ma­li­cious­ly pros­e­cut­ed for de­fraud­ing a hard­ware store of more than $850,000.
Last Tues­day, lawyers rep­re­sent­ing Nicole George filed the law­suit against the Of­fice of the At­tor­ney Gen­er­al and PC Dion Her­nan­dez, who laid 13 fraud charges against her in Feb­ru­ary 2022.
George was ac­cused of pay­ing for goods with 13 dis­hon­oured cheques.
Months be­fore Her­nan­dez laid the charges, the hard­ware store had filed a civ­il law­suit against George to re­cov­er the mon­ey.
While that case was pend­ing, George al­leged that the hard­ware store’s own­er had threat­ened her with a firearm.
She re­port­ed the in­ci­dent to the po­lice.
George made sev­er­al court ap­pear­ances in the crim­i­nal case be­fore a mag­is­trate dis­missed 12 of the charges. The re­main­ing charge was re­port­ed­ly dis­missed months lat­er, af­ter the Of­fice of the Di­rec­tor of Pub­lic Pros­e­cu­tions (DPP) ad­mit­ted that it could not sup­port the ba­sis or man­ner in which it had been brought.
Her­nan­dez re­port­ed­ly chal­lenged the out­come, but the ap­peal was even­tu­al­ly dis­con­tin­ued be­fore it was heard by a pan­el.
In court fil­ings ob­tained by Guardian Me­dia, George’s lawyers, led by Ravi Ra­j­coomar, SC, claimed that Her­nan­dez had no rea­son­able or prob­a­ble cause to charge her.
“Twelve of the 13 charges were statute-barred when laid, as was ap­par­ent on their face, and could not in law re­sult in a con­vic­tion,” they said.
“He (Her­nan­dez) did not him­self form any hon­est be­lief, on rea­son­able grounds, that the claimant was guilty of the of­fences charged,” they added.
They al­so point­ed out that George had paid $400,000 to­wards the debt be­fore the charges were laid.
They claimed that she had of­fered to pro­vide ev­i­dence of the pay­ments, but Her­nan­dez re­fused to con­sid­er it.
They fur­ther claimed that he failed to prop­er­ly in­ves­ti­gate the hard­ware store own­er’s al­leged threats, in­clud­ing an al­le­ga­tion that the own­er got his daugh­ter, a po­lice of­fi­cer, to “pub­lish her on so­cial me­dia”.
“Those threats were then car­ried out, by the charges and by the me­dia re­lease,” they said.
George’s lawyers claimed that her rep­u­ta­tion was se­vere­ly dam­aged when the Trinidad and To­ba­go Po­lice Ser­vice (TTPS) is­sued a press re­lease re­port­ing that she had been charged.
“The claimant has suf­fered and con­tin­ues to suf­fer de­pres­sion, se­vere anx­i­ety, chron­ic shame and sui­ci­dal ideation, with con­tin­u­ing dai­ly dis­tress and a loss of her sense of self,” they said.
“The dis­tress was great­ly in­creased by the ef­fect of the pub­lic­i­ty on her three daugh­ters, who were bul­lied at school and in need of med­ical and/or psy­cho­log­i­cal care as a re­sult,” they added.
They claimed that George’s se­cu­ri­ty com­pa­ny lost lu­cra­tive con­tracts as a re­sult of the charges and that busi­ness as­so­ciates re­fused to ac­cept her cheques as pay­ment.
They al­so al­leged that the charges af­fect­ed George’s stand­ing with her bankers, sev­er­al of whom with­drew fi­nanc­ing fa­cil­i­ties from her and her com­pa­ny.
They claimed that the with­draw­al of the fi­nanc­ing left a res­i­den­tial de­vel­op­ment in­com­plete and led to the clo­sure of a night­club.
“The un­fair and il­le­gal pub­li­ca­tion by the TTPS di­rect­ly re­sult­ed in the claimant’s loss of cred­it­wor­thi­ness and the fail­ure of her de­vel­op­ment and busi­ness­es,” they said.
George is al­so rep­re­sent­ed by Ryan Ra­j­coomar and Au­ro­ra Bharath.

The State has been or­dered to pay al­most $180,000 in com­pen­sa­tion to a man from Princes Town, who claimed that he was ex­tort­ed by a group of po­lice of­fi­cers.
In late April, the man, whose iden­ti­ty was with­held due to per­son­al safe­ty con­cerns raised by his at­tor­neys, ob­tained a de­fault judg­ment from High Court Judge Ava­son Quin­lan-Williams af­ter the Of­fice of the At­tor­ney Gen­er­al failed to de­fend his law­suit against the State.
The com­pen­sa­tion to be paid to him was as­sessed by High Court Mas­ter Wren­er­son Lochan late last month.
The law­suit stemmed from an in­ci­dent in Princes Town on March 2, 2024.
The man, a labour­er, was con­sum­ing a meal at a shop­ping mall when he was con­front­ed by a group of of­fi­cers in­clud­ing one he knew pre­vi­ous­ly.
He claimed that the of­fi­cers searched him and found 28 grammes of mar­i­jua­na (just short of the le­gal per­son­al lim­it) and $18,400 in cash.
He was hand­cuffed and placed in a po­lice ve­hi­cle.
He claimed that the of­fi­cers de­mand­ed that he sup­ply them with mar­i­jua­na for him to be re­leased.
He claimed that they took his cell­phone and at­tempt­ed to call con­tacts but could not do so as he had in­suf­fi­cient cred­it.
One of the of­fi­cers pur­chased a pre­paid phone card and then drove with the man to M1 Tasker Road.
While there, they con­tact­ed the man’s broth­er and re­quest­ed that he sup­ply the mar­i­jua­na and $10,000 to se­cure his re­lease.
His broth­er re­port­ed­ly claimed that he could pay the mon­ey but not sup­ply the mar­i­jua­na.
Al­though his broth­er de­liv­ered the cash at the lo­ca­tion iden­ti­fied by the of­fi­cers, the man was on­ly re­leased af­ter the of­fi­cers took his gold chain, val­ued at $189,000, and gold band, val­ued at $88,600.
The man went for med­ical treat­ment as he suf­fered in­juries to his wrists due to the hand­cuffs be­ing too tight.
He then made a re­port to the Pro­fes­sion­al Stan­dards Bu­reau (PSB).
In the law­suit, the man’s lawyers Dou­glas Bay­ley and Frank Git­tens claimed that the of­fi­cers breached sev­er­al of their client’s con­sti­tu­tion­al rights and caused him emo­tion­al dis­tress and phys­i­cal in­juries.
They claimed that he had been wrong­ful­ly ar­rest­ed, as­sault­ed and false­ly im­pris­oned.
They al­so al­leged un­just en­rich­ment and con­ver­sion in re­la­tion to the cash tak­en from him and his broth­er and the jew­ellery.
In de­cid­ing on the ap­pro­pri­ate com­pen­sa­tion for the man, Mas­ter Lochan did not award the full val­ue of the jew­ellery that he claimed was un­law­ful­ly tak­en by the of­fi­cers as he could not strict­ly prove such.
In­stead, he or­dered $40,000 for as­sault and bat­tery and false im­pris­on­ment; $18,400 in spe­cial dam­ages; $50,000 in nom­i­nal dam­ages; and $50,000 in ex­em­plary dam­ages.
He or­dered in­ter­est on the dam­ages and $19,784.59 in le­gal costs for pur­su­ing the lit­i­ga­tion.
The AG’s Of­fice was rep­re­sent­ed by Che Richards.

Po­lice ar­rest­ed 19 peo­ple and seized drugs, weapons, sus­pect­ed am­mu­ni­tion and house­break­ing im­ple­ments dur­ing sep­a­rate op­er­a­tions over the week­end in the South­ern, West­ern and East­ern Di­vi­sions.
In two re­leas­es is­sued yes­ter­day, the Trinidad and To­ba­go Po­lice Ser­vice re­port­ed 13 ar­rests dur­ing a 24-hour South­ern Di­vi­sion ex­er­cise un­der Op­er­a­tion RES­OLUTE Shield.

In St James, of­fi­cers stopped a Hyundai Ac­cent on Hen­ry Pierre Street on Sat­ur­day. Three men from Cas­cade were ar­rest­ed in con­nec­tion with the seizure of 15 pack­ets of sus­pect­ed ec­sta­sy weigh­ing 13.5 grammes.
In San­gre Grande, of­fi­cers ar­rest­ed three men dur­ing an op­er­a­tion which con­tin­ued in­to ear­ly yes­ter­day.
Po­lice re­port­ed find­ing house­break­ing im­ple­ments on the men and eight rounds of sus­pect­ed 9mm am­mu­ni­tion in a near­by Hon­da City.

Trinidad and To­ba­go has re­tained its Tier 2 rank­ing in the Unit­ed States De­part­ment of State’s 2026 Traf­fick­ing in Per­sons Re­port.
The des­ig­na­tion is un­changed from the 2025 re­port.
Tier 2 means the Gov­ern­ment does not ful­ly meet the min­i­mum stan­dards for the elim­i­na­tion of hu­man traf­fick­ing but is mak­ing sig­nif­i­cant ef­forts to do so.
The rank­ing fol­lows the coun­try’s re­moval from the Tier 2 Watch List in 2024, when the US State De­part­ment cit­ed in­creased ef­forts to in­ves­ti­gate and pros­e­cute traf­fick­ing cas­es and iden­ti­fy vic­tims.
The Tier 2 des­ig­na­tion does not mean traf­fick­ing has been elim­i­nat­ed. It in­di­cates that ef­forts are be­ing made to ad­dress the crime, while the min­i­mum stan­dards have not been ful­ly met.
In March, four Venezue­lan na­tion­als, in­clud­ing two mi­nors, were iden­ti­fied as traf­fick­ing vic­tims dur­ing a Counter Traf­fick­ing Unit op­er­a­tion at a prop­er­ty on Fras­er Street, Rio Claro.
In­ves­ti­ga­tors re­port­ed signs of pro­longed abuse, con­fine­ment and ex­ploita­tion.
Months lat­er, in May, two men were charged with a to­tal of 29 of­fences fol­low­ing the in­ves­ti­ga­tion, dubbed Op­er­a­tion Pur­ple Rain.
The charges in­clud­ed of­fences un­der the Traf­fick­ing in Per­sons Act, the Chil­dren Act and the Sex­u­al Of­fences Act. The mat­ter re­mains be­fore the courts.

Pro­mot­er Randy Glas­gow is call­ing on the Trin­ba­go Uni­fied Ca­lyp­so­ni­ans’ Or­gan­i­sa­tion (TU­CO) to take re­spon­si­bil­i­ty for main­tain­ing stat­ues ho­n­our­ing ca­lyp­so leg­ends, say­ing there is no rea­son to seek more Gov­ern­ment mon­ey when the art form al­ready re­ceives mil­lions in an­nu­al fund­ing.
His call fol­lows a vol­un­teer ef­fort on Sat­ur­day morn­ing to pow­er-wash the stat­ue of the Mighty Spar­row and clean its sur­round­ings.
Glas­gow said main­tain­ing the stat­ues of Spar­row and Lord Kitch­en­er should be­come part of TU­CO’s re­spon­si­bil­i­ties, rather than de­pend­ing on the Gov­ern­ment to pay for every cleanup.
He said he is al­so a mem­ber of TU­CO and be­lieves the or­gan­i­sa­tion has enough mem­bers to car­ry out the work.
“I feel, you know, there’s enough ca­lyp­so in there. I’m a mem­ber of TU­CO my­self, and there are like 500 TU­CO mem­bers, and, you know, that could be part of their man­date.”
Glas­gow said sim­i­lar at­ten­tion should be giv­en to the stat­ue of Lord Kitch­en­er.
He ar­gued that ca­lyp­so al­ready ben­e­fits from sub­stan­tial Gov­ern­ment sup­port.
“I don’t think it looks good if the min­istry al­ready plays its part, where every year, Ca­lyp­so get a sub­ven­tion of $15 to $16 mil­lion.”
He said seek­ing ad­di­tion­al mon­ey for rou­tine main­te­nance was un­nec­es­sary.
“I will nev­er en­cour­age that.”
The pro­mot­er said the cleanup was or­gan­ised by a small group of vol­un­teers who want­ed to en­sure Spar­row’s stat­ue re­mained in good con­di­tion fol­low­ing his death.
He said no one had asked him to be­come in­volved, but he felt a per­son­al re­spon­si­bil­i­ty to pro­tect Spar­row’s lega­cy.
“No­body asked me for any­thing and I just de­cid­ed, you know, be­cause I think I al­ways as­pire to pro­tect and pro­mote his lega­cy. And we have been do­ing that since the first day that he died.”
Glas­gow iden­ti­fied sev­er­al peo­ple in­volved in the ef­fort, in­clud­ing Luther, Hamidul­lah, ca­lyp­son­ian Twig­gy and Kurt, among oth­ers.
He said the group re­ceived sup­port from the May­or of Port-of-Spain, who arranged for a crew and wa­ter to as­sist with the cleanup.
The work in­clud­ed pow­er-wash­ing the stat­ue and cut­ting the sur­round­ing grass.
Glas­gow said main­tain­ing the area should not be dif­fi­cult and com­pared it to keep­ing a yard clean.
“I mean, you know, it’s a stat­ue and some bush to cut. It’s like a lit­tle yard in your home.”
He said the group hoped to con­tin­ue clean­ing the stat­ue reg­u­lar­ly, ide­al­ly once a month.
Glas­gow stressed that the stat­ue should re­main in good con­di­tion be­cause of its promi­nent lo­ca­tion near ma­jor ho­tels, Queen’s Hall and the Prime Min­is­ter’s Diplo­mat­ic Cen­tre.
“It’s cleaned up and paint­ed if nec­es­sary, but it must look good be­cause it’s a good lo­ca­tion.”
He said the vol­un­teers were com­mit­ted to en­sur­ing the stat­ue con­tin­ued to re­ceive at­ten­tion.
Glas­gow hopes the ini­tia­tive will en­cour­age greater re­spon­si­bil­i­ty among ca­lyp­so or­gan­i­sa­tions for pre­serv­ing mon­u­ments ho­n­our­ing the coun­try’s cul­tur­al icons.

As the en­tire coun­try awaits the grand open­ing of the new To­ba­go air­port ter­mi­nal to­mor­row, one dis­placed res­i­dent is still strug­gling to pick up the pieces.
Kay Pan­tin Solomon, 72, who now re­sides in Shir­van, says her re­lo­ca­tion has caused her con­sid­er­able trau­ma and left her in fi­nan­cial dis­tress.
Her stan­dard of liv­ing, she said, has been dras­ti­cal­ly re­duced, as she grap­pled with the death of her hus­band, an un­favourable will and sub-stan­dard work from con­trac­tors on her new home.
Pan­tin Solomon said her night­mare start­ed in 2019 when her hus­band died, leav­ing their guest­house to her step­son. De­spite the cir­cum­stances, Pan­tin Solomon said, through an at­tor­ney, she was able to get com­pen­sa­tion from the Gov­ern­ment. She said a space in Cove was pre­vi­ous­ly iden­ti­fied by her and her hus­band, but she did not have suf­fi­cient funds to buy it any­more.
Speak­ing to Guardian Me­dia last Thurs­day, the el­der­ly wid­ow said she felt tak­en ad­van­tage of by un­scrupu­lous con­trac­tors who took thou­sands of dol­lars and left her with a house falling apart.
“I is a woman. They know I don’t know bet­ter,” she said, as she point­ed to sig­nif­i­cant cracks on the walls of her home and the floor­ing. On one beam, chunks of con­crete had al­ready bro­ken away. She said win­dows were al­so dif­fi­cult to in­stall in some ar­eas as it would fur­ther desta­bilise the walls.
Af­ter liv­ing two years with­out elec­tric­i­ty as she strug­gled to re­build her life, the pen­sion­er is un­sure where she will find the funds to do re­pairs.
“I don’t have a TV in my house. I don’t have in­ter­net. I have no prob­lem re­lo­cat­ing, but as a wid­ow and sin­gle per­son, it re­al­ly hard.
“I can­not work. If they see a pen­sion­er get a lit­tle some­thing, they will take it away.”
She claimed Chief Sec­re­tary Far­ley Au­gus­tine had promised to pro­vide as­sis­tance, but she has yet to re­ceive it.
She said the phys­i­cal, fi­nan­cial and emo­tion­al stress of the sit­u­a­tion is tak­ing its toll.
“I had a guest­house, so com­ing from a guest­house to this, how could I ex­plain it?
“Is on­ly the God of heav­en that I serve that is keep­ing me, be­cause this is re­al­ly heart­break­ing, dev­as­tat­ing, for one in­di­vid­ual to go through by my­self. It very, very hard.”
Mean­while, an­oth­er res­i­dent, who wished to stay anony­mous, said re­set­tling in Shir­van was dif­fi­cult ow­ing to in­ad­e­quate com­pen­sa­tion and poor in­fra­struc­ture.
He said, “It have cer­tain things they didn’t put in place prop­er­ly for the res­i­dents. Watch the con­di­tion of the road. The road very bad. Grass grow­ing in the road. Watch the drainage block up by grass, and no­body com­ing here to cut it.”
He said the prices of steel and oth­er ma­te­ri­als went up con­sid­er­ably, leav­ing many res­i­dents un­able to prop­er­ly re­build their lives.
One dis­placed res­i­dent de­clined to speak about the sit­u­a­tion, her eyes welling up as she spoke briefly. She said talk­ing about their re­lo­ca­tion brought up mem­o­ries of the sen­ti­men­tal val­ue lost in their pre­vi­ous homes.
How­ev­er, she is hop­ing to ben­e­fit from one of the 50 hous­ing units promised by Au­gus­tine to those af­fect­ed. She al­so wel­comed Au­gus­tine’s in­vi­ta­tion for af­fect­ed res­i­dents to at­tend the air­port’s open­ing.
“I will go. I have to go there when I trav­el­ling any­way. I went when (for­mer prime min­is­ter Dr Kei­th) Row­ley had the (prac­ti­cal open­ing) cer­e­mo­ny last year, so I will at­tend,” she said.

Po­lice are search­ing for a woman who was re­port­ed­ly dragged from her car and bun­dled in­to a van by a stranger fol­low­ing a mi­nor road ac­ci­dent in Rousil­lac on Sat­ur­day.
Ac­cord­ing to a po­lice re­port, a 36-year-old truck dri­ver from South Oropouche was dri­ving a white Mac TGX along the South­ern Main Road, Rousil­lac, to­wards La Brea around 11.30 am when a sil­ver-grey Nis­san Sun­ny, dri­ven by an In­do-Trinida­di­an woman, al­leged­ly at­tempt­ed to over­take and squeeze be­tween his truck and an­oth­er ve­hi­cle.
The Sun­ny struck the truck, caus­ing dam­age. No one was in­jured.
The truck dri­ver stopped, got out and walked to­wards the Sun­ny, which had pulled over a short dis­tance away. He then saw a white H100 van trav­el­ling to­wards the La Brea dis­trict stop be­hind the car.
A thin, tall Afro-Trinida­di­an man wear­ing a black jer­sey and blue pants al­leged­ly jumped out of the van, ap­proached the Sun­ny, pulled the woman from the dri­ver’s seat and bun­dled her in­to the ve­hi­cle.
The van then turned around and sped off to­wards the Oropouche dis­trict.
The truck dri­ver re­port­ed the in­ci­dent, prompt­ing of­fi­cers from the High­way Pa­trol Unit, the South West­ern Di­vi­sion Task Force and the Crim­i­nal In­ves­ti­ga­tion De­part­ment to vis­it the scene and search for the H100. Their search was un­suc­cess­ful.
The An­ti-Kid­nap­ping Squad and La Brea CID have been alert­ed and pro­vid­ed with the truck dri­ver’s state­ment and the in­for­ma­tion gath­ered.
In­ves­ti­ga­tions are on­go­ing.
